d2.overview: Domain II maps the external rulebook: the laws that already reach AI (GDPR, non-discrimination, IP, consumer protection, product liability), AI-specific laws - the EU AI Act as the first comprehensive AI statute, plus South Korea's AI Basic Act and US federal and state AI laws (added in BOK v2.1) - and the voluntary standards and frameworks (OECD, NIST, ISO) that organizations use to operationalize trustworthy AI. The skill being tested is knowing which instrument applies to which situation, and what it actually requires.
d2.deep_dive:
Domain II is where the exam stops asking what AI governance **is** and starts asking what the law **requires**. It carries 19 to 23 of the 100 scored items, second only to Domains III and IV, and it splits into four competencies with different textures:

| Competency | Subject | Questions |
|---|---|---|
| **II.A** | How existing data privacy laws apply to AI | 4 to 6 |
| **II.B** | How other existing laws apply to AI (IP, non-discrimination, consumer protection, product liability) | 4 to 6 |
| **II.C** | Main elements of AI-specific laws (EU AI Act, Korea AI Basic Act, US federal and state) | 6 to 8 |
| **II.D** | Main industry standards and tools (OECD, NIST, ISO) | 3 to 5 |

### The organizing idea: which instrument applies

Almost every Domain II item is a matching problem. A fact pattern is described and the task is to name the instrument that governs it, the obligation it triggers, or the role that carries it. The instruments fall into three families:

- **Law that already reaches AI without naming it.** The GDPR, the US fair-lending and civil-rights statutes, the FTC Act, copyright and product liability all predate AI and apply to it anyway. II.A and II.B are about seeing the hook.
- **Law written for AI.** The EU AI Act is the first comprehensive statute, with South Korea's AI Basic Act and a growing set of US state laws behind it. II.C is about knowing the mechanism.
- **Voluntary standards and frameworks.** The OECD Principles, the NIST AI RMF and its Playbook, and ISO/IEC 22989, 42001 and 42005. None bind, but regulators, auditors and contracts increasingly treat them as the measure of due care. II.D is about knowing which instrument does what.

### Currency: as enacted versus as amended

Domain II is the domain where the calendar matters most, and the repo's convention is to state which legal state a fact describes. Two examples carry most of the weight:

- **The EU AI Act.** As enacted (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), Annex III high-risk rules applied from 2 August 2026 and Annex I product-embedded rules from 2 August 2027. As amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force 27 July 2026), those dates moved to 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028. 2 August 2026 still starts Article 50 transparency and the Commission's GPAI enforcement, and 2 December 2026 brings two new Article 5 prohibitions.
- **US non-discrimination.** Federal agencies pulled back from disparate-impact enforcement through 2025 and 2026 (EEOC guidance withdrawn, Executive Order 14281, the CFPB's Regulation B rule effective 21 July 2026), but the statutes and private suits are unaffected. An executive order cannot amend Title VII.

BOK v2.1 was approved on 9 September 2025, before the Omnibus was agreed, so a live exam item may quote either timeline. Read each stem for its anchor ("as originally enacted" or "as amended by the 2026 Digital Omnibus"); if there is none, ask whether the fact being tested changed at all.

### What changed in BOK v2.1

- **II.C** was renamed from "the main elements of the EU AI Act" to "the main elements of AI-specific laws", its weight rose from 5 to 7 questions to 6 to 8, and the domain introduction now names South Korea's AI Basic Act and US federal and state AI laws.
- **II.A**'s first indicator became "transparency, choice, lawful basis", widening the focus from consent to every Article 6 basis, and controller obligations now name automated decision-making explicitly.
- **II.D** dropped NIST ARIA and added ISO/IEC 42005 to the core ISO list, so the core three are 22989, 42001 and 42005. Its weight fell from 4 to 6 questions to 3 to 5.

### How to work a Domain II question

Name the instrument first, then the role, then the duty. A question about a hiring tool may be testing Title VII, the GDPR's Article 22, the EU AI Act's Annex III, or NYC Local Law 144, and the fact pattern usually contains the one detail that decides which. Precision about dates and status (adopted, in force, draft, proposed, withdrawn, on appeal) is worth as much as knowing the rules themselves.
d2.exam: The second-heaviest domain at roughly 19 to 23 questions. The EU AI Act is the single most-tested instrument - risk tiers, prohibited practices, high-risk obligations, GPAI rules, penalties and the implementation timeline all appear - and it is the only place the exam asks you to compare jurisdictions, so expect Korea and US state law items too. GDPR questions focus on its AI pressure points: Article 22 automated decision-making (with SCHUFA and Dun & Bradstreet Austria), Article 9 special categories, Article 35 DPIAs, Article 28 processor contracts, and the EDPB's 2024-2026 position on models and scraping. II.B is scenario matching (fact pattern to doctrine), and II.D is instrument matching (function to framework).
key_points: Spans four knowledge areas: privacy/data protection law, other existing (sectoral and civil) laws, AI-specific laws (EU AI Act, Korea AI Basic Act, US federal and state AI laws), and AI standards and frameworks
EU AI Act risk ladder: unacceptable (banned), high-risk (heavy obligations), limited (transparency), minimal (largely unregulated)
Penalty anchors: EUR 35m/7% for prohibited practices, EUR 15m/3% for high-risk non-compliance, EUR 7.5m/1% for misleading information, all 'whichever is higher'
Existing law reaches AI even without 'AI' in its name: ECOA and Title VII for discrimination, FTC Act for deception, product liability for defects
Standards stack: OECD principles (values), NIST AI RMF (risk process), ISO/IEC 42001 (certifiable management system), ISO/IEC 23894 (risk guidance, background only)
State which legal state a fact describes: 'as enacted' (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) versus 'as amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI' (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force 27 July 2026)
BOK v2.1 widened II.C beyond the EU and moved the domain's centre of gravity toward AI-specific law; II.C now carries the most questions of the four competencies

ch4.overview: This knowledge area applies privacy and data protection law to AI. Core doctrines - transparency, choice, lawful basis, purpose limitation, data minimization, privacy by design - collide with AI's appetite for repurposed data and its ability to infer what was never collected. It also covers controller obligations (DPIAs, processor contracts, cross-border transfers, data subject rights, automated decision-making, breach notification, records) and the extra rules for sensitive or special-category data such as biometrics.
ch4.deep_dive:
II.A carries 4 to 6 questions and is four indicators, each mapping onto a section of the knowledge area.

### 1. Transparency, choice, lawful basis and purpose limitation

A privacy notice must disclose purposes, data categories, legal basis, retention, recipients and whether decisions are made solely by automated means. AI strains each: models are opaque, they **infer** sensitive facts from ordinary inputs, they change behaviour after collection, they pull from many sources, and controller/processor lines blur across a supply chain.

**Consent** must be freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous, given by a clear affirmative act and as easy to withdraw as to give, with the burden of proof on the controller. Pre-ticked boxes, bundling and dark patterns all fail. Consent is one of six Article 6 bases, not the default, and there is no hierarchy among them.

**Purpose limitation** (Article 5(1)(b)) is AI's chronic problem: data collected to deliver a service cannot be silently repurposed to train a model, and a secondary use needs a compatibility assessment or a fresh basis. **Lawful basis** for training is usually contested on legitimate interest (Article 6(1)(f)), because consent does not scale. EDPB Opinion 28/2024 applies a three-step test: a real and present interest, necessity (no less intrusive route, proportionate data), and a balancing test in which data subjects' reasonable expectations carry weight. The EDPB's draft Guidelines 03/2026 on web scraping say consent "would most probably not be" workable at that scale and that legitimate interest is the usual basis, and they repeat that special-category data needs an Article 9(2) exception **as well as** an Article 6 basis. The Commission's proposed AI-specific legitimate-interest article (Article 88c) is still a proposal, not law.

### 2. Data minimization and privacy by design

Article 5(1)(c) requires data that is adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary. AI's pull toward large datasets and overcollection runs against it, so minimization is applied stage by stage: limit scope at collection, drop non-contributing features and mask sensitive fields at preprocessing, train with privacy-preserving methods (federated learning, differential privacy), and limit inputs at inference.

**Privacy by design** (given legal force by Article 25) embeds protection from the outset: proactive not remedial, privacy as the default, embedded into design, full functionality, end-to-end security, visibility and transparency, and respect for the user. In practice: DPIAs at problem framing, privacy-preserving training and fairness validation during development, then retention limits, contestability and drift monitoring in operation.

**Anonymisation is a high bar.** Under EDPB Opinion 28/2024 a model trained on personal data is anonymous only if it is insignificantly likely that anyone could extract a training subject's data from it, directly or through queries, judged case by case. The draft Guidelines 02/2026 propose three tests: no record isolation, no linkage, no inference. Removing names is pseudonymisation, not anonymisation.

### 3. Controller obligations

The controller determines the purposes and means of processing (Article 4(7)) and owes the accountability duty to **demonstrate** compliance (Article 5(2)). A **DPIA** (Article 35) is required for processing likely to result in high risk, which AI triggers through automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects, large-scale special-category data, systematic profiling, monitoring of public areas, or vulnerable populations.

Third-party **processors** (cloud, training, foundation models, labelling, AI-as-a-Service) need an Article 28 data processing agreement covering subject matter, data types, security, sub-processing, rights and DPIA assistance, deletion and audit rights. Watch for **processor drift**, where a vendor's continuous training quietly widens processing beyond instructions.

**Cross-border transfers** need an adequacy decision, standard contractual clauses, binding corporate rules or a derogation, and remote **access** from outside the EEA counts even if no data is stored there. After Schrems II, SCCs and BCRs require a transfer impact assessment.

**Data subject rights** meet their hardest cases here: access (Article 15) must explain black-box outputs, erasure (Article 17) struggles with weights, and objection (Article 21) collides with profiling. **Article 22** prohibits decisions based **solely** on automated processing with legal or similarly significant effects unless a contract, law or explicit consent allows it, and even then the controller owes safeguards including meaningful human intervention. Two CJEU rulings define the doctrine: **SCHUFA** (C-634/21, 2023) holds a credit bureau's score is itself an Article 22 decision when the lender draws strongly on it, so upstream score and model providers can owe the duties; **Dun & Bradstreet Austria** (C-203/22, 2025) holds Article 15(1)(h) means a concise, intelligible account of the procedure and principles actually applied, not a formula dump, with claimed trade secrets weighed by the DPA or court. **Breach notification** (Article 33) requires telling the supervisory authority within 72 hours and affected individuals without undue delay where risk is high, with AI-specific vectors (training-data leakage, inversion and membership inference, output regurgitation, model poisoning) that standard DLP misses.

### 4. Sensitive and special-category data

Article 9 forbids processing special-category data (biometrics for identification, health, genetic, racial or ethnic origin, religion, political opinions, union membership, sex life or orientation) unless a narrow exception applies, with explicit consent the usual one. AI makes this harder three ways: deliberate use (health records), incidental collection (a CV tool harvesting political affiliation), and **inference**, where a model deduces a protected characteristic from inputs that never contained it, and the inference still triggers Article 9. Heightened protection for biometrics attaches when the data is used to **uniquely identify** a person, so categorisation without identity linkage may fall outside Article 9 but still carries bias risk. As amended by the 2026 Digital Omnibus on AI, a new AI Act Article 4a adds an AI Act basis for special-category data used strictly to detect and correct bias, on top of the GDPR.
ch4.exam: GDPR is the reference statute: anchor articles by number - 5 (principles), 6 (lawful bases), 9 (special categories), 22 (automated decisions), 25 (privacy by design), 28 (processors), 33 (breach notice), 35 (DPIAs). Scenario questions test whether a processing operation needs consent or another lawful basis, when a DPIA is mandatory, what secondary use of training data requires, and what safeguards an automated decision needs. Expect the two CJEU rulings to appear: SCHUFA (a decisive score is itself an Article 22 decision) and Dun & Bradstreet Austria (access means an intelligible explanation of the logic actually applied). EDPB Opinion 28/2024 supplies the three-step legitimate-interest test and the rule that models are not automatically anonymous; the 2026 anonymisation and web-scraping guidelines are drafts, so an answer that treats them as settled law is wrong.
key_points: Purpose limitation is AI's chronic pain point: data collected for service delivery cannot be silently repurposed for model training without a compatibility assessment or a fresh basis
Data minimization applies to models too: if 15 features perform like 50, use 15, and train with federated learning or differential privacy where raw data is not needed

GDPR Article 22 grants the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal or significant effects, with narrow exceptions and required safeguards including meaningful human intervention
DPIAs are required for high-risk processing - systematic profiling, large-scale special categories, automated decisions with significant effects - and AI routinely triggers them
Special categories (health, biometrics, race and more) need an Article 9 condition; AI can infer them from ordinary inputs, and the inference triggers Article 9 even though nothing was collected
Controllers must bind processors with Article 28 DPAs covering instructions, security, sub-processors, rights assistance, deletion and audit, and must watch for processor drift

SCHUFA (2023) makes a decisive third-party score an Article 22 decision; Dun & Bradstreet Austria (2025) requires an intelligible explanation of the logic actually applied, with trade secrets weighed by the regulator or court
Models are not automatically anonymous: EDPB Opinion 28/2024 sets the extraction test, and removing names is pseudonymisation, not anonymisation

ch5.overview: This knowledge area surveys the sectoral and civil laws that reach AI without naming it: intellectual property (training-data copyright, output ownership, trade secrets), non-discrimination law (disparate impact through proxies), consumer protection (deception and unfairness), and product liability (defective AI as a product). The lesson is that 'no AI law here' never means 'no law here'.
ch5.deep_dive:
II.B carries 4 to 6 questions and is the domain's scenario-matching exercise: read the fact pattern, name the doctrine. It is substantively unchanged from BOK v2.0.1.

### 1. Intellectual property

IP meets AI at three points: inputs (training on protected works), the model itself (whether weights contain copies), and outputs (whether generated content infringes or can be owned).

In the **US**, training is tested under the four fair-use factors (purpose and character, nature of the work, amount used, effect on the market). District courts split in 2025: training was fair use on the records in **Bartz v. Anthropic** and **Kadrey v. Meta** (both June 2025), but not in **Thomson Reuters v. Ross** (February 2025), where the use built a competing market substitute. No US appellate court had ruled as of September 2026. Two details decide cases: **how the data was acquired** (Bartz refused to excuse a permanent library of pirated books, and the case settled for USD 1.5 billion, final approval 20 July 2026) and **whether market harm was proven** (Kadrey won on a thin record, not a safe harbour). Outputs matter too: **GEMA v. OpenAI** (Munich, November 2025) held memorised lyrics were reproductions in the model and in outputs, outside the TDM exception, and pinned responsibility on the operator. **Authorship is human**: *Thaler v. Perlmutter* (D.C. Cir., March 2025; cert. denied 2 March 2026) requires a work authored in the first instance by a human being, and prompts alone are not enough, though human selection, arrangement and modification of AI output can be protected (Copyright Office Part 2).

In the **EU** there is no fair use, only the DSM Directive's exceptions: Article 3 for research organisations and heritage institutions with no opt-out, and Article 4 for anyone with lawful access, subject to machine-readable rights reservations under Article 4(3). GPAI providers must honour those reservations and publish a training-content summary (AI Act Article 53(1)(c)-(d)), wherever training happened and even for open-source models. The UK treated model weights as not an infringing copy (*Getty v. Stability AI*, November 2025, on appeal) while Munich treated memorised works as reproduced in the parameters (*GEMA*): the split is live. **Trade secrets** protect datasets, architecture, hyperparameters and prompts only while genuinely secret.

### 2. Non-discrimination

Two theories: **disparate treatment** (intentional, including deliberate use of a prohibited-basis proxy) and **disparate impact** (a neutral practice that disproportionately harms a protected group, no intent required). Title VII section 703(k) writes the disparate-impact standard into the statute: the plaintiff shows the practice causes the impact, the employer must show it is job-related and consistent with business necessity, and the plaintiff can still win by showing a less discriminatory alternative. Sector hooks: **Title VII, ADA and ADEA** in employment; **ECOA** (with Regulation B adverse-action reasons) and **FCRA** in credit; the **Fair Housing Act** in housing and mortgage lending; state insurance law for insurance. **Proxy variables** (postal code for race, credit history for race) are the recurring mechanism.

Federal enforcement retreated in 2025 and 2026: the EEOC withdrew its AI technical assistance, Executive Order 14281 directed agencies to minimise disparate-impact liability, the CFPB withdrew its AI circulars, and a final Regulation B rule effective **21 July 2026** states that ECOA does not provide for the effects test. But an executive order cannot amend a statute, HUD's removal of its FHA effects rule is proposed not final, and private plaintiffs, states and the FHA route (via *Inclusive Communities*, 2015) remain.

### 3. Consumer protection

**FTC Act section 5** prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices, without proof of intent. AI enforcement has targeted deception about what AI can do: Operation AI Comply (September 2024, including DoNotPay) and Workado (April 2025) for unsubstantiated accuracy claims. The FTC set aside its Rytr order in December 2025 because the theory condemned a tool for possible misuse, but deception remains squarely enforceable. Every state has a "mini-FTC Act" (California UCL, Massachusetts 93A, New York GBL 349). AI-specific risks: undisclosed AI interaction, **dark patterns** that personalise manipulation at scale, deepfake impersonation and fabricated endorsements, and AI-generated fake reviews, which the FTC's Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule (August 2024) bans.

### 4. Product liability

Three theories: **design defect** (manufactured as intended but unreasonably dangerous), **manufacturing defect** (deviates from the intended design), and **failure to warn**. They run through strict liability (defective and caused harm, no negligence needed), negligence, or breach of warranty. AI complicates defect analysis because behaviour is dynamic, models drift, and outputs are probabilistic. The EU settled the "is software a product" debate: under the revised **Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853**, software including AI is a product however supplied, liability is no-fault, disclosure can be ordered once a claim is plausible, and defect and causation can be **presumed** where technical or scientific complexity makes proof excessively difficult, with machine learning a named example. Member States must transpose by **9 December 2026**, and it applies to products placed on the market after that date. The fault-based **AI Liability Directive was withdrawn** (OJ C/2025/5423, 6 October 2025), so an answer that relies on its presumption of causality is wrong.

### The through-line

Identify the doctrine, then the actor, then the specific duty. Acquisition source, market-dilution evidence, competing substitute, training location and memorisation are the one-fact deciders in IP; proxy review, business necessity and specific adverse-action reasons are the ones in discrimination.
ch5.exam: Scenario-heavy: an AI credit model with disparate impact (ECOA and fair lending), a chatbot making deceptive claims (FTC Act), a generative model trained on copyrighted works (the fair-use fight), an autonomous product causing injury (strict liability versus negligence). Match the fact pattern to the doctrine, and then to the actor. Watch the case-status traps: Thaler is final (cert. denied 2 March 2026), Bartz is settled (USD 1.5 billion, approved 20 July 2026), and Ross, Getty and GEMA are on appeal; NYT v. OpenAI is pending. Remember that withdrawn guidance or an executive order does not repeal a statute, and that the AI Liability Directive was withdrawn, so answers resting on its presumption of causality are wrong.
key_points: Copyright: training on protected works turns on fair use in the US (courts split in Bartz, Kadrey and Ross) and on the DSM Article 3 and Article 4 exceptions in the EU; purely AI-generated output lacks copyright without human authorship
Acquisition matters: pirated or shadow-library sources drive exposure, and Bartz settled for USD 1.5 billion after the court refused to excuse a permanent library of pirated books
Disparate impact doctrine catches facially neutral models that harm protected classes through proxy variables (zip code to race), and Title VII section 703(k) writes the standard into the statute
Key US anti-discrimination hooks: Title VII and the ADA in employment, ECOA with Regulation B in credit, the Fair Housing Act in housing, state law in insurance
FTC Act section 5 reaches AI: deceptive claims about AI capabilities (Workado, DoNotPay), unfair algorithmic practices and dark patterns, with no intent required
Product liability theories against AI are manufacturing defect, design defect and failure to warn; strict liability does not require proving negligence
EU Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853 treats software including AI as a product, adds rebuttable presumptions of defect and causation, and must be transposed by 9 December 2026
The AI Liability Directive was withdrawn (OJ C/2025/5423, 6 October 2025): there is no EU fault-based AI liability regime

ch6.overview: BOK v2.1 II.C covers the main elements of AI-specific laws. The EU AI Act is the anchor: risk tiers (prohibited, high, limited, minimal), a heavy compliance chain for high-risk systems, transparency duties, a separate GPAI regime, role-based obligations and GDPR-scale penalties. Under v2.1 the subdomain also covers South Korea's AI Basic Act and US federal and state AI laws that apply to private-sector organizations. The EU AI Act was amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force 27 July 2026), which moved the high-risk dates and simplified several duties.
ch6.deep_dive:
II.C carries 6 to 8 questions, the most of the four competencies, and BOK v2.1 widened it from "the EU AI Act" to "AI-specific laws". The EU AI Act is the anchor; Korea and the US states are the comparison.

### Risk classification

The EU AI Act regulates by risk, not by technology:

| Tier | Test | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Prohibited** | Unacceptable risk to rights or safety | Banned outright (Article 5) |
| **High-risk** | Annex I safety components, or Annex III use cases | Full Chapter III obligations chain |
| **Limited** | Interaction or synthetic content | Transparency duties (Article 50) |
| **Minimal** | Negligible risk | No new obligations; voluntary codes |

As enacted, Article 5(1) lists eight prohibitions: subliminal or purposefully manipulative techniques, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, individual criminal-offence risk prediction, untargeted facial-image scraping, emotion recognition in workplaces and education, biometric categorisation by sensitive traits, and real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces (with narrow law-enforcement exceptions). As amended by the 2026 Omnibus it lists ten: from 2 December 2026, AI that generates or manipulates realistic intimate or sexual imagery of an identifiable person without explicit consent ("nudification") and AI that generates child sexual abuse material (Article 5(1)(ba)-(bb)). High-risk arrives by two routes: a safety component of a product under EU harmonisation law (Annex I), or an Annex III use case (biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services including credit, law enforcement, migration, justice). The tier is contextual, and a deployer that substantially modifies a system becomes its provider.

### The high-risk obligations chain

A high-risk provider owes a documented risk-management system across the lifecycle; data governance (relevant, representative training, validation and test data, as free from bias as possible); technical documentation; automatic logging; instructions for use; human oversight designed for detection, override and shutdown; accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity; a quality management system; a conformity assessment (internal control or a notified body) with CE marking; EU database registration; and post-market monitoring with serious-incident reporting. Deployers owe human oversight in use, input-data quality, log retention and incident reporting; importers and distributors verify CE marking and documentation and cooperate with authorities. Article 50 transparency applies from **2 August 2026**: chatbots must disclose that they are AI and synthetic output must be marked in machine-readable form, and deployers must disclose deepfakes, emotion-recognition and biometric-categorisation use, and AI-generated text on matters of public interest unless human-reviewed. Generative systems already on the market before 2 August 2026 have until **2 December 2026** for marking.

### General-purpose AI

All GPAI providers owe technical documentation and downstream information (Article 53(1)(a)-(b)), a copyright policy honouring Article 4(3) opt-outs, a public training-content summary (Article 53(1)(c)-(d)), and, for non-EU providers, an EU authorised representative (Article 54). Open-source models are exempt only from points (a) and (b), and not at all if they have systemic risk. A model is **presumed** to have systemic risk above 10^25 FLOP of training compute (Article 51(2)), or may be designated by the Commission using the Annex XIII criteria; the provider must then notify the Commission, run documented adversarial evaluation, assess and mitigate Union-level risks, report serious incidents and maintain adequate cybersecurity (Article 55). The Act requires adversarial testing to be conducted and documented, not published; "external audits" and public red-team reports are Code of Practice extras, not Article 55 duties.

### Enforcement and penalties

The **European AI Office** (in the Commission) supervises GPAI and holds exclusive competence under Article 88; as amended it is also exclusively competent for AI systems built on a GPAI model by the same provider or group (with carve-outs) and for AI in DSA very large online platforms and search engines. **National competent authorities** run market surveillance for everything else, with inspection, corrective-order, withdrawal and recall powers. Penalty ceilings: **EUR 35m or 7%** for prohibited practices; **EUR 15m or 3%** for most other breaches, including Commission GPAI fines under Article 101; **EUR 7.5m or 1%** for incorrect or misleading information, all "whichever is higher". SMEs get the lower of the two figures on every tier, and as amended small mid-caps get the lower cap on the two lower tiers only.

### Timeline: as enacted versus as amended

| Date | As enacted (2024/1689) | As amended (2026/1744) |
|---|---|---|
| 2 Feb 2025 | Prohibitions (eight) and AI literacy | Same (softened literacy wording from 27 Jul 2026) |
| 2 Aug 2025 | GPAI obligations, governance, penalty regime except Article 101 | Same |
| 2 Aug 2026 | Annex III high-risk, Article 50, Commission GPAI enforcement | Article 50 and GPAI enforcement only |
| 2 Dec 2026 | - | Two new prohibitions; Article 50(2) marking deadline for legacy generative systems |
| 2 Dec 2027 | - | Annex III high-risk rules |
| 2 Aug 2028 | - | Annex I product-embedded high-risk rules |

BOK v2.1 predates the Omnibus, so an item may quote the original dates. Read the stem for its anchor; prohibitions, GPAI dates and penalty ceilings did not change.

### Beyond the EU

**South Korea's AI Basic Act** (in force 22 January 2026) is lighter and promotion-first: no prohibited practices, duties on "high-impact AI" operators to run a risk-management plan, provide explanations, protect users and keep records for five years, a **best-efforts** impact assessment, transparency and labelling for generative AI, and fines capped at KRW 30 million for only three failures. **US law** is a patchwork: no comprehensive federal statute, but state and local laws that reach private organizations, including Colorado's SB 26-189 ADMT regime (effective 1 January 2027), Texas TRAIGA, California's SB 53 and SB 942, Utah's SB 149 and SB 226, Illinois HB 3773, New York's RAISE Act, and NYC Local Law 144's bias audits.
ch6.exam: 6 to 8 questions, up from 5 to 7 under BOK v2.0.1. Expect tier classification (spot the prohibited practice, place a use in Annex III), the high-risk obligations chain, GPAI versus systemic-risk GPAI duties, the provider/deployer/importer/distributor split, and the penalty ladder. Date items may follow the original AI Act text, so learn both columns: as enacted, Annex III high-risk applied 2 August 2026 and Annex I 2 August 2027; as amended, 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028. 2 August 2026 still starts Article 50 and Commission GPAI enforcement, and 2 December 2026 brings the two new prohibitions. Since II.C now covers AI-specific laws generally, expect at least one comparative item on Korea's lighter, best-efforts regime or a US state law.
key_points: Risk tiers: prohibited (Article 5), high-risk (Annex I products and Annex III uses), limited-risk transparency (Article 50), minimal risk
Prohibitions: eight as enacted, from 2 February 2025; the 2026 Omnibus adds intimate-imagery and CSAM bans from 2 December 2026, for ten in total

High-risk provider chain: risk management, data governance, documentation, logging, instructions, human oversight, accuracy and security, QMS, conformity assessment, CE mark, registration, post-market monitoring

GPAI: all providers owe documentation, downstream information, a copyright policy and a training-content summary; systemic-risk models (presumed above 10^25 FLOP) add notification, adversarial evaluation, risk mitigation, incident reporting and cybersecurity

Penalties: EUR 35m/7% for prohibitions; EUR 15m/3% for most obligations and Commission GPAI fines; EUR 7.5m/1% for misleading information; lower-figure caps for SMEs on every tier and for small mid-caps on the two lower tiers
Timeline as amended: Article 50 and GPAI enforcement 2 August 2026; Annex III high-risk 2 December 2027; Annex I high-risk 2 August 2028
Roles decide obligations: deployers that substantially modify a system become providers, and importers are liable for placing non-compliant systems on the market

Beyond the EU: South Korea's AI Basic Act (best-efforts, KRW 30m fines, no prohibitions) and a US patchwork (Colorado, Texas, California, Utah, Illinois, New York, NYC) invite comparison of tiers, roles and enforcement

ch7.overview: This knowledge area tours the voluntary standards and frameworks that turn principles into practice: the OECD AI Principles (the intergovernmental values baseline, with its classification framework, AI-system definition and incident definitions), NIST's AI RMF with its Govern-Map-Measure-Manage cycle and the Playbook's per-subcategory suggested actions, the Generative AI Profile, and the core ISO standards BOK v2.1 names - 22989 (terminology), 42001 (certifiable AI management system) and 42005 (AI system impact assessment). None are law, but regulators, auditors and contracts increasingly treat them as the de facto measure of due care.
ch7.deep_dive:
II.D carries 3 to 5 questions (down from 4 to 6 in v2.0.1). It is instrument matching: a function is described and you name the framework. BOK v2.1 lists exactly three core ISO standards (22989, 42001, 42005), dropped NIST ARIA, and reaches into the OECD's working tools as well as its principles.

### OECD: the values baseline

The **OECD Recommendation on Artificial Intelligence** (OECD/LEGAL/0449), adopted **22 May 2019**, was the first intergovernmental AI standard. The OECD Council revised its **AI system definition on 8 November 2023** and the Recommendation more broadly on **3 May 2024**. It is not binding: adherents (47 as of September 2026, the EU among them) make a political commitment. Five values-based principles: inclusive growth, sustainable development and well-being; respect for the rule of law, human rights and democratic values, including fairness and privacy; transparency and explainability; robustness, security and safety; and accountability. Five recommendations for policy makers cover R&D investment, an inclusive AI ecosystem, interoperable governance, human capacity, and international co-operation.

The 2023 definition matters because the EU AI Act's Article 3(1) closely tracks it: a machine-based system that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers from the input it receives how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments. The five edits were "explicit or implicit" objectives, inference from input, "content" added to outputs, "physical" replacing "real", and adaptiveness after deployment.

The OECD's tools go past the principles. The **Framework for the Classification of AI Systems** (February 2022) has five dimensions: People and Planet, Economic Context, Data and Input, AI Model, and Task and Output; a trap worth knowing is that **action autonomy** is a Task and Output criterion, not an AI Model one. The **incident and hazard definitions** (May 2024) separate an AI incident (realised harm to health, critical infrastructure, rights or property) from an AI hazard (an event that could plausibly lead to one, with near misses counting), with serious incidents, disasters and serious hazards as narrower tiers. The **AI Incidents and Hazards Monitor (AIM)** tracks publicly reported events, and the **Hiroshima AI Process Reporting Framework** (OECD-hosted since February 2025) lets organizations report against the G7 Code of Conduct in a common format.

### NIST: the risk process

The **NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0** (January 2023) is voluntary, rights-preserving and sector-agnostic. It frames AI risk as contextual (the same system is high-risk in one deployment and low-risk in another), emergent, opaque and societal in scale. Four core functions:

- **GOVERN** - the cross-cutting foundation: policies, roles and accountabilities, risk tolerance and appetite, and a risk-aware culture with escalation channels.
- **MAP** - context and risk identification: intended purpose and foreseeable misuse, system design and data, stakeholders and affected populations, and prioritised risks including epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty.
- **MEASURE** - ongoing evaluation: metrics, testing (unit, red team, stress), monitoring and logging, and documented reporting.
- **MANAGE** - response: risk treatment (accept, transfer, avoid, mitigate), incident response and recovery, integration with cybersecurity, privacy and enterprise risk, and retirement planning.

Seven trustworthiness characteristics run through it: valid and reliable; safe; secure and resilient; accountable and transparent; explainable and interpretable; privacy-enhanced; and fair with harmful bias managed. The **AI RMF Playbook** supplies suggested actions, documentation prompts and references for all 72 subcategories, and the **Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)** tailors the RMF to generative AI. NIST ARIA, an evaluation programme with model, red-team and field testing, was a II.D indicator in v2.0.1 but is background only under v2.1.

### ISO: the core three

**ISO/IEC 22989:2022** is the terminology standard: 110 or more defined concepts covering the AI lifecycle, ML paradigms, system roles (AI provider, manufacturer, customer, subject) and trustworthiness properties. It defines, and does not prescribe. **ISO/IEC 42001:2023** is the world's first certifiable AI management system standard, built on the Annex SL structure (context, leadership, planning, support, operation, performance evaluation, improvement) and the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle, modelled on ISO 27001 and ISO 9001. Impact assessment is a requirement, not an option: clause 6.1.4 defines the process, clause 8.4 performs it, and Annex A objective A.5 adds controls. **ISO/IEC 42005:2025** is the guidance on how to do that assessment: a process (clause 5) and a record (clause 6) covering the system, its data, its deployment environment, interested parties, and both benefits and harms, kept under review and reassessed when intended use, the system or the legal context changes. It is guidance, not certifiable, and it feeds but does not replace a GDPR Article 35 DPIA or an EU AI Act Article 27 FRIA.

Two distractors: **ISO/IEC 42006:2025** sets requirements for the bodies that certify against 42001 (it regulates the certifiers, not the certified), and **ISO/IEC 23894:2023** is AI risk-management guidance extending ISO 31000. The split to remember: 23894 asks about risk to the organization; 42005 asks about impacts on people.

### How they fit

Read the stack as a progression: the OECD supplies values, the NIST AI RMF supplies a risk process, the Playbook supplies how-to actions, ISO/IEC 22989 supplies the vocabulary, ISO/IEC 42001 supplies the certifiable management system that holds it all, and ISO/IEC 42005 supplies the impact assessment of a specific system. A question asking which instrument to use for a given job is asking you to place it on that ladder.
ch7.exam: 3 to 5 questions under BOK v2.1. Match the instrument to its function: values to the OECD; risk process to the NIST AI RMF; how-to actions to the Playbook; vocabulary to ISO 22989; a certifiable management system to ISO 42001; impact assessment of a specific system to ISO 42005. Know the four RMF functions and the seven trustworthiness characteristics cold. Remember NIST ARIA was removed in v2.1, that the core ISO list is a closed set of three, and that 42005 is guidance rather than certifiable. The OECD's tools are fair game: the five classification dimensions, incident versus hazard, and which 2023 definition edit did what.
key_points: OECD AI Principles (2019, revised 2023 and 2024): the first intergovernmental AI standard, non-binding, 47 adherents; the 2023 AI-system definition and the 2022 classification framework sit alongside
NIST AI RMF 1.0 (January 2023): voluntary and non-certifiable; Govern then Map, Measure, Manage; seven trustworthiness characteristics
NIST AI RMF Playbook: suggested actions, documentation prompts and references for all 72 subcategories, named in the BOK
ISO/IEC 42001: the certifiable AI management system (AIMS), Annex SL structure, PDCA, the audit and certification target
ISO/IEC 42005: guidance (not certifiable) for assessing a specific AI system's impacts on people and society, complementing 42001's impact-assessment requirement
ISO/IEC 22989 defines the shared vocabulary; 23894 (AI risk management) is background only in v2.1, as is NIST ARIA
OECD tools beyond the principles: the five-dimension classification framework, incident versus hazard definitions, and the Hiroshima reporting framework
Distinguish 42005 from 42006: 42005 is impact-assessment guidance; 42006 sets requirements for the bodies that certify against 42001

t_consent.overview: The front door of data protection applied to AI: people must know (notice) and often agree (consent, choice) to how their data is used, and every use must honour the purpose it was collected for (purpose limitation). AI strains all three, because models are opaque, they infer what was never collected, and training is a tempting second use for data gathered for something else.
t_consent.deep_dive:
This topic is the first II.A indicator, and it is three doctrines that lean on each other.

### Notice

Notice means telling people how their data will be collected, used, stored and shared. For AI it must also disclose whether decisions are made solely by automated means. The required content: purposes, data categories, legal basis, retention periods, recipients, and the automated-decision fact.

AI makes notice hard in six ways: opaque black-box logic, **inference** (creating sensitive facts from ordinary inputs), dynamic behaviour (a model that keeps learning uses data differently after collection), many data sources with unclear provenance, automated decision-making that Article 22 does not fully reach, and accountability gaps where controller and processor roles blur across a supply chain. A good AI notice is plain-language and layered, explains the AI's role in the decision, says whether a human is in the loop, and tells people how to access, contest or opt out. Burying "we train models on your data" on page 40 of a privacy policy is not notice, and it draws both regulator and FTC attention.

### Choice and consent

Valid consent is freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous, given by a clear affirmative act, revocable, and recorded, with the burden of proof on the controller. Explicit consent is the higher bar required for special-category data and high-risk uses; implicit consent is generally insufficient for AI; opt-in is the GDPR default and opt-out is available only in limited jurisdictions. Four obstacles recur: power imbalance (people cannot refuse an essential service), lack of understanding (nobody comprehends what a deep model will infer), opacity, and **dark patterns** (pre-ticked boxes, hidden opt-outs, biased defaults, the illusion of choice). Consent is one of six Article 6 bases, not the default, and there is no hierarchy among them.

### Purpose limitation

Article 5(1)(b) requires data collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed incompatibly. **Purpose creep** is the gradual widening of use beyond the original purpose, and it is endemic in AI where data is reused across product features, R&D, monetisation and unrelated prediction. Training is a separate purpose from inference, third-party models arrive with undisclosed training data, and users are rarely told what downstream purposes a model serves. The cure is a **compatibility assessment** for each secondary use, separate datasets for distinct tasks, dataset documentation aligned to intended use, and updated notices at every material change.

### How the three fit

Notice tells; choice empowers; purpose limitation constrains. An exam scenario usually breaks one of the three: a repurposed dataset (purpose), a coerced or bundled consent (choice), or an undisclosed automated decision (notice).
t_consent.exam: Scenarios probe whether repurposing data for AI training needs fresh notice and consent or a compatibility analysis, and what valid consent requires (freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous, and as easy to withdraw as to give). The recurring trap is treating consent as the default basis: it is one of six, and legitimate interest is often the real basis for training. A second trap is bundling consent with a service or hiding it behind a dark pattern, which fails the free and specific tests.
key_points: Purpose limitation: data collected to deliver a service cannot be silently diverted to train models - a compatibility assessment or a new lawful basis is required
GDPR-valid consent is freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous and as easy to withdraw as to give; bundled or coerced consent fails
Notice must actually inform: burying AI training in page 40 of a privacy policy invites regulator and FTC attention
Consent is one lawful basis among several (contract, legitimate interests, legal obligation) - choose deliberately and document the choice
Secondary use is the recurring AI sin: assess compatibility, or obtain fresh consent, before repurposing
AI inference creates sensitive data from ordinary inputs, so notice and consent must cover what the model deduces, not only what was collected

t_minimization.overview: Two design principles that fight AI's instincts: collect only what the purpose needs (data minimization, GDPR Article 5(1)(c)), and build protection in from the start rather than bolting it on (privacy by design, Article 25). Both push toward fewer features, narrower collection, privacy-preserving training methods, and demonstrable limits on identifiability.
t_minimization.deep_dive:
### Data minimization

Article 5(1)(c) requires personal data that is adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the stated purpose. AI runs against it: model development wants large datasets, exploration is open-ended, and teams overcollect against a hypothetical future use. The practical answer is to minimize at each stage:

| Stage | Minimization move |
|---|---|
| Collection | Limit scope; avoid sensitive data unless strictly necessary; do not collect on speculation |
| Preprocessing | Drop non-contributing features; mask or redact sensitive fields |
| Training | Use federated learning or differential privacy so raw personal data is not centralised |
| Inference | Limit model input to the minimal feature set the task needs |

The framing to remember is "smart data, not big data": collection discipline (reduce scope and volume) plus technical safeguards (reduce identifiability). If 15 features perform like 50, use 15.

### Privacy by design

Privacy by design, formulated by Ann Cavoukian and given legal force by Article 25, has seven principles: proactive not reactive; privacy as the default; embedded into design; full functionality (positive-sum, not privacy versus utility); end-to-end security; visibility and transparency; and respect for the user. Applied to AI it maps onto the lifecycle: DPIAs and necessity tests at problem framing; privacy-preserving training, bias detection and interpretability during development; retention limits, contestability and drift monitoring in operation. In MLOps it means privacy checks in CI/CD, privacy linting, model cards that record privacy characteristics, and drift detection.

### Techniques

Data masking and tokenisation, pseudonymization, on-device processing, homomorphic encryption (compute on encrypted data), federated learning (data stays local, only model updates are shared), differential privacy (no single record can be reconstructed from outputs), and synthetic data. Synthetic data is not privacy-preserving by default: overfitted generators can leak, and small populations stay vulnerable.

### Anonymisation is a high bar

Removing names is **pseudonymisation**, not anonymisation. Under EDPB Opinion 28/2024 a model trained on personal data is anonymous only if it is insignificantly likely that anyone could extract a training subject's data, directly or through queries, assessed case by case against the controller's documentation. The draft Guidelines 02/2026 propose three tests: no record isolation, no linkage, no inference, and note that anonymity can differ from one holder to another.
t_minimization.exam: The minimization questions are usually the easiest points in II.A if you resist the bait: 'more data always improves the model' is wrong, and 'collect now, decide the purpose later' is wrong. Know the stage-by-stage moves and the technique-to-problem mapping (federated learning and differential privacy for training without centralising raw data; homomorphic encryption for computing on encrypted data). For privacy by design, remember it is a legal requirement under Article 25, not just good practice, and that pseudonymisation is not anonymisation.
key_points: Data minimization (Article 5(1)(c)): adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary - the '50 features but 15 perform equally, use 15' scenario
Minimize stage by stage: scope at collection, features at preprocessing, raw data at training, inputs at inference
Privacy by design (Article 25): proactive, default-on, embedded, full-functionality, end-to-end secure, visible and transparent, user-centric

Privacy-preserving techniques map to problems: federated learning and differential privacy for training, homomorphic encryption for computing on encrypted data, masking and tokenisation for stored data
Synthetic data is not automatically privacy-preserving: overfitting can leak, and small populations remain identifiable
Removing names is pseudonymisation, not anonymisation; EDPB Opinion 28/2024 sets an extraction test before a model counts as anonymous

t_controller.overview: The controller determines the purposes and means of processing (Article 4(7)) and carries the accountability duty to demonstrate compliance (Article 5(2)). For AI that means DPIAs for high-risk processing, Article 28 contracts with processors, transfer safeguards for cross-border flows, answers to data subject rights, safeguards for automated decisions, breach notification and records.
t_controller.deep_dive:
### Who is the controller

The controller is the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing; a processor acts on the controller's behalf. In AI supply chains the line blurs: a cloud or model vendor that keeps training on customer data, or a black-box AI-as-a-Service platform with little configuration, can become a **joint controller**. The accountability principle (Article 5(2)) means controllers must not only comply but be able to **demonstrate** it.

### DPIAs (Article 35)

A Data Protection Impact Assessment is required where processing is likely to result in high risk. AI triggers it through automated decision-making with legal or similarly significant effects, large-scale special-category data, systematic profiling, monitoring of publicly accessible areas, and vulnerable populations. A DPIA describes the processing and its purpose, the training and operational data at field level, the applicable laws, necessity and proportionality, the risks from the data subject's perspective, the mitigations, and any consultation. The common AI pitfalls are unclear system boundaries (model versus business logic), framing technical risk instead of human impact, and never revisiting the DPIA once a model keeps learning.

### Processors (Article 28)

Every processor relationship needs a binding data processing agreement: subject matter, duration, nature and purpose; data types and data subjects; security and confidentiality; sub-processing rules; assistance with rights requests and DPIAs; return or deletion at the end; and audit rights. Watch for **processor drift**, where a vendor's continuous training or new features widen processing beyond instructions, and for clauses that let a vendor train on the controller's data.

### Cross-border transfers

Transfers outside the EEA need an adequacy decision, standard contractual clauses, binding corporate rules or a derogation, and remote **access** from outside the EEA counts even if nothing is stored there. After Schrems II, SCCs and BCRs require a transfer impact assessment weighing the destination's surveillance law and any supplementary measures.

### Data subject rights

| Right | Article | AI challenge |
|---|---|---|
| Access | 15 | explaining black-box outputs |
| Rectification | 16 | correcting data baked into weights |
| Erasure | 17 | deletion from trained models |
| Restriction | 18 | halting use in continuous learning |
| Object | 21 | profiling is intrinsic to many systems |
| Automated decisions | 22 | opt-out and genuine human review |

**Article 22** prohibits decisions based **solely** on automated processing with legal or similarly significant effects unless a contract, law or explicit consent permits it, and even then the controller owes safeguards including meaningful human intervention, not rubber-stamping. Two CJEU rulings define the doctrine: **SCHUFA** (C-634/21, 2023) holds that a credit bureau's score is itself an Article 22 decision when the lender draws strongly on it, so upstream providers owe the duties; **Dun & Bradstreet Austria** (C-203/22, 2025) holds that Article 15(1)(h) means a concise, intelligible account of the logic actually applied, not an algorithm dump, with claimed trade secrets weighed by the DPA or court.

### Breach notification and records

Article 33 requires notifying the supervisory authority within 72 hours of awareness and Article 34 requires telling affected people without undue delay where risk is high. AI adds vectors that standard DLP misses: training-data leakage through inversion or membership inference, output regurgitation, model poisoning, and silent degradation. Article 30 records of processing and the Article 5(2) accountability duty supply the paper trail: data flow diagrams, model and system cards, consent and purpose logs, DPIAs and transfer assessments.
t_controller.exam: Anchor the articles: 4(7) controller, 5(2) accountability, 28 processors, 30 records, 33 and 34 breach, 35 DPIAs, 44 to 49 transfers. Scenario questions test when a DPIA is mandatory, what an Article 28 contract must contain, and whether a transfer safeguard is adequate. Article 22 items pair with the two rulings: a decisive third-party score is itself an automated decision (SCHUFA), and an access request about it needs an intelligible explanation of the logic applied, not a formula (Dun & Bradstreet Austria).
key_points: Controller determines purposes and means (Article 4(7)); accountability (Article 5(2)) means being able to demonstrate compliance, not just assert it
DPIA (Article 35) is required for high-risk processing: automated decisions with significant effects, large-scale special categories, systematic profiling, public-area monitoring, vulnerable people
Article 28 processor contracts must cover instructions, security, sub-processing, rights and DPIA assistance, deletion and audit rights
Cross-border transfers need adequacy, SCCs, BCRs or a derogation; remote access counts as a transfer, and Schrems II requires a transfer impact assessment
Article 22 bans solely automated decisions with legal or significant effects absent a contract, law or explicit consent, and even then requires meaningful human intervention
SCHUFA (2023): a decisive credit score is itself an Article 22 decision; Dun & Bradstreet Austria (2025): access means an intelligible account of the logic actually applied
Breach notification: supervisory authority within 72 hours (Article 33), affected people without undue delay if high risk (Article 34)
AI-specific breach vectors include training-data leakage, membership inference, output regurgitation and model poisoning, which standard DLP misses

t_sensitive.overview: GDPR Article 9 forbids processing special-category data (biometrics for identification, health, genetic, racial or ethnic origin, religion, political opinions, union membership, sex life or orientation) unless a narrow exception applies. AI makes this harder because it can infer these traits from inputs that never contained them, and the inference triggers the same protection.
t_sensitive.deep_dive:
### The default prohibition

Article 9 starts from a ban, not a permission: special-category data may be processed only under a narrow exception, with **explicit consent** the usual one (freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous, affirmative, documented). Others include employment and social protection law, vital interests, substantial public interest, public health, archiving and research with safeguards, and legal claims. Consent and contract are not interchangeable: sensitive data under Article 9(2)(a) must be explicit and revocable, whereas contract necessity is a demanding test that nice-to-have features fail.

### What counts as sensitive

Biometrics used for identification, health and genetic data, racial or ethnic origin, religious or philosophical beliefs, political opinions, trade union membership, and sex life or sexual orientation. Jurisdictions differ at the edges: the CPRA adds precise geolocation; Brazil's LGPD, Canada's PIPEDA and India's DPDP Act track similar lists. Financial data, government identifiers and children's data carry extra protection by context.

### AI's risk profile

Three ways AI meets sensitive data: **deliberate** (a health tool using medical records), **incidental** (a CV sorter harvesting political affiliation from past activism), and **inferential**, where a model predicts ethnicity, health or orientation without ever being told it. The risk set is lack of a valid basis, discrimination and bias, opacity, surveillance and chilling effects.

### Biometrics and the identification line

Biometric data is especially sensitive because it cannot be changed if compromised. The GDPR's heightened protection attaches only where biometric data is used to **uniquely identify** a person, so categorisation alone (say, age estimation without identity linkage) may fall outside Article 9, though it still carries ethical and discrimination risk. Facial recognition for retail surveillance is the classic trigger.

### Inference is the trap

Inferential privacy violations arise when models deduce religious affiliation from language, sexual orientation from social-graph connections, health conditions from wearable data, or political leaning from browsing history. The important rule: these inferences can trigger Article 9 even though the attribute was never explicitly collected. Controllers are responsible for downstream inferences, and sensitive-by-proxy features (postal code, credit history, education) can smuggle protected traits back in.

### The AI Act overlay

As amended by the 2026 Digital Omnibus on AI, a new AI Act Article 4a adds an AI Act basis for special-category data used strictly to detect and correct bias, on top of the GDPR, with strict-necessity safeguards (no effective alternative data, pseudonymisation, access controls, no onward transfer, deletion and records).
t_sensitive.exam: Expect a scenario where a system infers a protected trait and the question is whether Article 9 applies. The answer is usually yes: inference counts. Know the exceptions, that explicit consent is the high bar for sensitive data, and the biometrics distinction between identification (Article 9) and categorisation (may fall outside it, but still risky). Article 9 data also needs an Article 6 basis as well as the Article 9(2) exception, a point the EDPB's web-scraping draft repeats.
key_points: Article 9 starts from prohibition: special-category data needs a narrow exception, with explicit consent the usual one
Sensitive means biometrics for identification, health, genetic, race and ethnicity, religion, political opinions, union membership, sex life and orientation
AI meets sensitive data deliberately, incidentally and inferentially, and the inference of a protected trait triggers Article 9 even without collection
Biometric protection attaches to identification, not mere categorisation, but categorisation still carries bias and ethical risk
Sensitive data needs an Article 9(2) exception as well as an Article 6 basis for the processing
New AI Act Article 4a (via the 2026 Omnibus) adds an AI Act basis for special-category data used strictly to detect and correct bias, with strict-necessity safeguards

ref_gdpr.overview: The General Data Protection Regulation (EU 2016/679): the world's most influential data protection law and, until the AI Act, the EU's main lever over AI. For AI governance its pressure points are Article 22 automated decisions, Article 9 special categories, Article 5 purpose limitation and minimization, Article 25 privacy by design, Article 28 processors, Article 35 DPIAs and Article 33 breach notice.
ref_gdpr.deep_dive:
### What it is and why it matters for AI

The GDPR governs the processing of personal data of people in the EU. It has extraterritorial reach (Article 3): it applies to controllers and processors outside the EU that offer goods or services to EU people or monitor their behaviour. For AI that means a model trained or deployed anywhere can fall inside it if EU people are affected, and it was the EU's principal AI regulator until the AI Act arrived.

### The articles AI governance leans on

| Article | Rule |
|---|---|
| 5 | principles: lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, minimization, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity, accountability |
| 6 | six lawful bases, no hierarchy |
| 9 | special-category prohibition and exceptions |
| 13 to 15 | transparency and access, including automated-decision logic |
| 17 and 21 | erasure and objection, which reach profiling |
| 22 | solely automated decisions with legal or significant effects |
| 25 | privacy by design and by default |
| 28 | processor contracts |
| 33 and 34 | breach notification (72 hours; individuals if high risk) |
| 35 | DPIAs for high-risk processing |
| 44 to 49 | cross-border transfers |

### The AI pressure points

Three doctrines carry most AI questions. **Article 22** bans solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects unless a contract, law or explicit consent allows them, and even then requires safeguards including meaningful human intervention; the CJEU's **SCHUFA** (2023) and **Dun & Bradstreet Austria** (2025) rulings extend the duty up the vendor chain and define what an explanation must contain. **Article 9** protects special-category data, and AI's ability to infer such traits from ordinary inputs brings the inference inside the ban. **Purpose limitation and minimization** collide with training's appetite for repurposed and over-collected data.

### Enforcement and penalties

Two fine tiers: up to EUR 10m or 2% of global annual turnover, and up to EUR 20m or 4%, whichever is higher, depending on the breach. National supervisory authorities enforce, coordinated by the EDPB, which also issues the guidance that shapes AI practice: Opinion 28/2024 on AI models and the 2026 drafts on anonymisation and web scraping.

### Status discipline

The EDPB's 2026 anonymisation and web-scraping guidelines are **drafts** (consultation to 30 October 2026), not final. The Commission's Digital Omnibus GDPR amendments, including a narrower personal-data definition and an AI-specific legitimate-interest article (Article 88c), are **proposals**, not law. Apply the GDPR as it stands, and say so when a fact depends on a draft or a proposal.
ref_gdpr.exam: The second-most-tested law after the AI Act. Anchor articles by number and expect the two fine tiers (up to EUR 20m or 4% for the top tier). The AI-specific items cluster on Article 22 (with SCHUFA and Dun & Bradstreet Austria), Article 9 inference, Article 35 DPIAs and Article 28 processors. Status traps are common: an answer that treats the EDPB's 2026 anonymisation or web-scraping guidelines as final law, or the Digital Omnibus GDPR changes as in force, is wrong.
key_points: Article 5 principles: lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimization; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality; accountability
Article 22: right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects, with narrow exceptions and safeguards including human intervention
Article 35 DPIAs for likely-high-risk processing; consult the supervisory authority if risk remains high (Article 36)
Data subject rights versus AI: access includes meaningful information about automated decision-making logic; erasure and objection extend to profiling
Breach regime: notify the DPA within 72 hours (Article 33); notify individuals when risk is high (Article 34)
Penalties: two tiers, up to EUR 10m/2% and up to EUR 20m/4% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher
Extraterritorial scope (Article 3): applies to processing of EU people's data by controllers anywhere when offering goods or services or monitoring behaviour
The EDPB's 2026 anonymisation and web-scraping guidelines are drafts and the Digital Omnibus GDPR changes are proposals: apply the GDPR as it stands

t_ip.overview: IP law meets AI at three points: inputs (training on copyrighted works, tested under US fair use and the EU text and data mining exceptions), the model itself (whether weights contain copies of the works), and outputs (whether generated content infringes, and whether it can be owned). Trade secrets protect the model only while it is genuinely secret.
t_ip.deep_dive:
### The three touchpoints

Inputs, the model, and outputs. Each raises a different question: was copying the works to train lawful; does a trained model contain copies; does an output infringe or attract copyright of its own.

### Fair use in the US

Training is tested under the four fair-use factors: purpose and character (transformative or duplicative), nature of the work, amount used, and effect on the market (including dilution by competing output). District courts split in 2025: training was fair use on the records in **Bartz v. Anthropic** and **Kadrey v. Meta** (both June 2025), and not fair use in **Thomson Reuters v. Ross** (February 2025), where the model was trained on a competitor's headnotes to build a market substitute. No US appellate court had ruled as of September 2026; the Ross appeal was argued in the Third Circuit on 11 June 2026.

Two facts decide cases. **Acquisition**: Bartz refused to excuse a permanent central library of pirated books, and the case settled for USD 1.5 billion (final approval 20 July 2026). **Market harm**: Kadrey won only because the plaintiffs offered no dilution evidence, so the ruling is not a safe harbour.

### Human authorship

*Thaler v. Perlmutter* (D.C. Cir., 18 March 2025; cert. denied 2 March 2026) holds the Copyright Act requires a work authored in the first instance by a human being, so an AI system cannot be the author. Prompts alone are not enough, but human selection, arrangement and modification of AI output can be protected (Copyright Office Part 2, January 2025). Applicants must disclose AI-generated content and exclude more-than-de-minimis AI material.

### The EU: TDM, not fair use

There is no fair use in the EU. The DSM Directive gives two text and data mining exceptions: **Article 3** for research organisations and cultural heritage institutions, with no opt-out (contract terms overriding it are unenforceable), and **Article 4** for anyone with lawful access, for any purpose including commercial training, but only if the rightholder has not reserved the right "in an appropriate manner, such as machine-readable means" (Article 4(3)). GPAI providers must honour those reservations and publish a public, sufficiently detailed training-content summary (AI Act Article 53(1)(c)-(d)), and recital 106 makes that apply regardless of where training happened; open-source models are not exempt from those two points.

### Does the model contain copies?

The courts disagree, and both leading decisions are on appeal. *Getty v. Stability AI* (UK High Court, [2025] EWHC 2863 (Ch), 4 November 2025) held that a model which does not store or reproduce the works is not an "infringing copy", and Getty dropped its training and outputs claims. *GEMA v. OpenAI* (Regional Court Munich I, 11 November 2025) held that lyrics memorised in the model were reproductions in the model and in outputs, that the TDM exception covers building the training corpus and not memorisation, and that the operator (not the user) is responsible for outputs from simple prompts. Copyright is territorial, so where training happened matters.

### Trade secrets

Trade secret law protects proprietary datasets, architecture, hyperparameters, fine-tuning methods and prompts, but only while they are genuinely secret. Transparency duties collide with secrecy: the AI Act's training-content summary is meant to be comprehensive in scope rather than technically detailed, taking trade secrets into account.
t_ip.exam: Expect scenario items that turn on one fact: how the data was acquired (Bartz), whether the plaintiff proved market harm (Kadrey), whether the use built a competing substitute (Ross), where training happened (Getty), or whether the model memorised (GEMA). Watch the status traps: Thaler is final, Bartz is settled, and Ross, Getty and GEMA are on appeal. Remember that fair use and the EU's TDM exceptions are different regimes: a US developer that places a GPAI model on the EU market must still honour Article 4(3) opt-outs.
key_points: US fair use is decided case by case: training was held fair on the records in Bartz and Kadrey (June 2025) and rejected in Thomson Reuters v. Ross (February 2025); the Ross appeal, argued in the Third Circuit on 11 June 2026, is undecided
Acquisition matters: Bartz refused to excuse a central library of pirated books, and the case settled for USD 1.5 billion (final approval 20 July 2026)

Human authorship is required: Thaler v. Perlmutter (D.C. Cir. 2025, cert. denied 2 March 2026); prompts alone are not enough, but human selection, arrangement and edits are protectable (Copyright Office Part 2)
EU: DSM Article 3 (research organisations and heritage institutions, no opt-out) versus Article 4 (anyone, subject to machine-readable opt-outs for online content)
AI Act Article 53(1)(c)-(d): GPAI providers need a copyright policy honouring Article 4(3) opt-outs and a public training-content summary, wherever training happened and even for open-source models

Models as copies: Getty v. Stability AI (UK, November 2025) held weights that store no works are not an infringing copy; GEMA v. OpenAI (Munich, November 2025) held memorised lyrics were reproductions outside the TDM exception; both are on appeal
Trade secrets protect models, weights and prompts only while they are genuinely kept secret

t_nondiscrim.overview: Anti-discrimination law reaches AI through two theories: disparate treatment (intentional, including deliberate use of a proxy for a protected trait) and disparate impact (a neutral practice that disproportionately harms a protected group, with no intent required). The sector hooks are Title VII and the ADA in employment, ECOA and FCRA in credit, the Fair Housing Act in housing, and state law in insurance.
t_nondiscrim.deep_dive:
### Two theories

**Disparate treatment** is intentional discrimination, including the deliberate use of a variable that stands in for a protected class. **Disparate impact** needs no intent: a facially neutral practice that disproportionately harms a protected group is unlawful unless it is justified. AI produces disparate impact readily, through biased training data, proxy variables, feedback loops and sampling bias.

### The Title VII standard

Title VII section 703(k) (42 U.S.C. 2000e-2(k)) writes the disparate-impact standard into the statute: the plaintiff shows a particular practice causes the impact, the employer must then show the practice is job-related and consistent with business necessity, and the plaintiff can still win by showing a less discriminatory alternative the employer refuses to adopt. Because the standard is in the statute, an executive order or withdrawn agency guidance cannot remove it. Employers are responsible for the selection procedures they use even if a third-party vendor built the tool, and vendor disclaimers do not shield liability.

### Credit and lending

The **Equal Credit Opportunity Act** prohibits discrimination in credit on protected bases. Two AI-facing duties: no intentional discrimination or deliberate proxy use, and specific **principal reasons for adverse action** (12 CFR 1002.9), which means explainability. Saying an applicant "failed to achieve a qualifying score" is not enough; the reasons must relate to and accurately describe the factors actually considered. The **Fair Credit Reporting Act** governs third-party consumer data: a communication bearing on creditworthiness used for credit, insurance or employment can be a consumer report, and adverse action based on one triggers notice, the credit score, the reporting agency's details and dispute rights. A CFPB final rule effective **21 July 2026** states that ECOA does not provide for the effects test, so federal ECOA disparate-impact liability is gone; intentional discrimination and deliberate proxies remain unlawful.

### Housing

The **Fair Housing Act** prohibits discrimination in sale, rental and financing. It reaches discriminatory ad targeting (differential exposure), discriminatory impact, and failure to monitor third-party tools. The Supreme Court recognised FHA disparate impact in *Texas Dept. of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project* (2015). HUD proposed on 14 January 2026 to remove its discriminatory-effects regulations and supplemented that on 10 August 2026, but neither is final, and the Act-based theory does not depend on HUD's rule. Mortgage lending is covered by both ECOA and the FHA, so the FHA route survives the 2026 Regulation B change.

### Insurance

No single federal statute; states regulate. Colorado's SB21-169 was the first to require insurers to test AI for unfair discrimination and document governance. Proxy variables (postal code, education, occupation, credit history) are the recurring mechanism.

### The 2025 to 2026 federal pullback

The EEOC removed its AI technical assistance on 27 January 2025; Executive Order 14281 (23 April 2025) directed agencies to minimise disparate-impact liability; the CFPB withdrew its AI circulars on 12 May 2025; and the Regulation B rule followed. The governance takeaway: federal agencies stepped back, but the statutes, private plaintiffs, states and the FHA route remain, so keep testing for disparate impact and documenting proxy review.
t_nondiscrim.exam: Scenario items name a sector and ask which statute applies: Title VII and the ADA in hiring, ECOA and Reg B in credit, FCRA for third-party scores, the FHA in housing and mortgage lending, state law in insurance. Know the three-step Title VII disparate-impact test and that it is statutory. A recurring trap is the 2025 to 2026 federal pullback: withdrawn guidance and an executive order do not repeal a statute, and ECOA's effects test being removed from Regulation B does not remove FHA disparate impact.
key_points: Disparate treatment is intentional (including deliberate proxy use); disparate impact needs no intent and is the theory AI most often triggers

ECOA requires specific principal reasons for adverse action (12 CFR 1002.9), which forces explainability; a 'qualifying score' statement is insufficient
FCRA treats third-party algorithmic scores as consumer reports when used for credit, insurance or employment, triggering notices and dispute rights
Fair Housing Act disparate impact (Inclusive Communities, 2015) survives the 2026 Regulation B change and still covers mortgage lending
Proxy variables (postal code, credit history, education, occupation) are the recurring mechanism and must be tested and justified
2025 to 2026 pullback: EEOC guidance removed, Executive Order 14281, CFPB circulars withdrawn, Regulation B effects test removed - but the statutes, states and private plaintiffs remain
