term:CE Marking.deep_dive:
CE marking is the visible sign that a product meets the EU harmonisation legislation that applies to it. Article 48 requires the high-risk AI provider to affix the CE marking to the AI system, or to its packaging or the accompanying documentation, so that it is visible, legible and indelible. Digital CE marking is permitted. The marking follows the general principles of Regulation (EC) 765/2008.

Two distinctions carry the exam marks. First, **CE marking is the provider's own act**. It is not issued by a notified body; where a notified body is involved, its four-digit identification number is placed next to the marking. The legal weight comes from the EU Declaration of Conformity (Article 47) that the provider signs, which states that the requirements are met. Second, the sequence matters: conformity assessment (Article 43), then the Declaration of Conformity (Article 47), then CE marking (Article 48), then database registration (Article 49).

Failing to affix the CE marking when required falls under the operator obligations of Article 16 and is enforceable at the Article 99(4) tier: up to **EUR 15 million or 3%** of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. For SMEs and start-ups the fine is capped at the lower of the two figures.
term:CE Marking.exam_tip: CE marking (Article 48) is the provider's own declaration, affixed after the EU Declaration of Conformity (Article 47); it is not a certificate from a notified body. Remember the order: assessment, declaration, CE mark, registration.

term:AI Provider.deep_dive:
Article 3(3) defines a provider as a person or entity that develops an AI system or a general-purpose AI model, or that has one developed, and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name or trademark, whether for payment or free of charge. The role turns on **who puts the system out under their own name**, not on who wrote the code.

The provider is the pivot of the AI Act: it carries the core obligations in Article 16, including the risk-management system (Article 9), data governance (Article 10), technical documentation (Article 11), conformity assessment (Article 43), the EU Declaration of Conformity (Article 47), CE marking (Article 48) and registration (Article 49).

The role can move down the supply chain. Under Article 25, a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party becomes a provider when it puts its own name or trademark on a high-risk system, substantially modifies such a system, or modifies its intended purpose in a way that leaves it high-risk. That is why a company that rebrands or retrains a vendor's model takes on the full provider obligations rather than staying a deployer.

Contrast the other roles: a **deployer** (Article 3(4)) uses the system under its own authority; an **importer** (Article 3(6)) places a third-country provider's system on the Union market; a **distributor** (Article 3(7)) makes it available further down the chain.
term:AI Provider.exam_tip: A provider puts the system on the market under its own name or trademark (Article 3(3)). Article 25 is the trap: rebranding, substantially modifying or repurposing a high-risk system makes you the provider.

term:AI Distributor.deep_dive:
Article 3(7) defines a distributor as any entity in the supply chain, other than the provider or the importer, that makes an AI system available on the Union market. The distributor's obligations under Article 24 are deliberately lighter than the importer's, because the distributor does not introduce the system to the market; it passes on a system someone else has already placed there.

Before making a high-risk system available, the distributor must verify that:

- it bears the CE marking;
- it is accompanied by the EU Declaration of Conformity and instructions for use;
- the provider and, where applicable, the importer have complied with their identification duties.

If a distributor believes or has reason to believe that a system is not compliant, it must not make it available until it is brought into conformity, and it must inform the provider or importer. It must also take corrective action, withdraw or recall where required, and cooperate with authorities.

The clean line for the exam: the **importer places** a third-country system on the Union market and verifies it; the **distributor makes available** a system already on the market and checks that the markings and documents are present. The distributor does not repeat the conformity assessment.
term:AI Distributor.exam_tip: Distributor (Article 3(7), Article 24): in the supply chain but neither provider nor importer, making the system available. It verifies CE marking, the declaration of conformity and instructions; it does not redo the conformity assessment.

term:Watermarking.deep_dive:
Article 50(2) of the EU AI Act requires providers of AI systems that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text to mark the output in a **machine-readable format** and make it detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. The duty sits on the provider, and it is a technical marking duty rather than a notice aimed at a human reader.

Watermarking is one provenance technique among several. Others are metadata attached to the file, fingerprinting that identifies a model from patterns in its output, and cryptographic signatures or content credentials such as the C2PA standard. Marking survives copying better than a visible label, but it is not tamper-proof, and the Act sets an effectiveness standard rather than naming a technology.

Timing matters. Article 50 applies from **2 August 2026**. As amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744), generative systems already on the market before that date have until **2 December 2026** to add the Article 50(2) marking, a grace period written into the new Article 111(4).

Two related duties sit alongside marking: deployers who create deepfakes must disclose that the content is artificial (Article 50(4)), and providers whose systems interact directly with people must say so (Article 50(1)). Marking is the provider's machine-readable duty; disclosure is the human-facing duty.
term:Watermarking.exam_tip: Article 50(2) puts machine-readable marking on the **provider** of a generative system; deepfake disclosure under Article 50(4) falls on the **deployer**. Marking applies from 2 August 2026, with 2 December 2026 for legacy generative systems.

term:Nudification and CSAM Prohibitions.deep_dive:
Points (ba) and (bb) were added to Article 5(1) by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) and apply from **2 December 2026**. They close a gap the Commission's Article 112 review flagged in May 2026.

- **(ba) Non-consensual intimate imagery.** AI that generates or manipulates realistic images, video, audio or similar material of an identifiable person's intimate parts, or of that person in sexually explicit activity, without their explicit consent. This is the practice sometimes called nudification.
- **(bb) Child sexual abuse material.** AI that generates or manipulates material within the meaning of Article 2(c) and (e) of Directive 2011/93/EU.

Scope is drawn carefully in the new Article 5(1a) and (1b). **Placing on the market** is caught only where the prohibited output is the system's intended purpose, or where it is a reasonably foreseeable and reproducible outcome that the system lacks reasonable safeguards to prevent. **Use** is caught only where the deployer uses the system for that purpose. Editing that does not increase a person's exposure or change the sexual nature of existing material is not manipulation.

These are Article 5 prohibitions, so they carry the top fine tier: up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover (Article 99(3)). The carve-outs spare general-purpose tools and legitimate photo editing from a blanket ban while catching purpose-built abuse generators.
term:Nudification and CSAM Prohibitions.exam_tip: The two 2026 Omnibus bans, Article 5(1)(ba) and (bb), apply from 2 December 2026. Placing on the market is caught only where the output is the intended purpose, or a foreseeable, reproducible result the system does not guard against.

term:Code of Practice on Marking and Lab.deep_dive:
The Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content is the voluntary instrument that sits under Article 50(7) of the EU AI Act. The final version was published on **10 June 2026**, after the Commission and the AI Board judged it adequate.

It has two sections:

- **Section 1 (providers)**: machine-readable marking of synthetic output and the detection measures that go with it, supporting the Article 50(2) duty.
- **Section 2 (deployers)**: labelling of deepfakes and of AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, supporting the Article 50(4) duties.

By the end of July 2026 about **190 organizations** had signed. The Commission made EU icons available for the labels. A code of practice is one way to demonstrate compliance; it is not law and it does not bind non-signatories.

Keep three instruments apart, because exam items mix them:

- the **Article 50 guidelines** (published 20 July 2026) are the Commission's non-binding interpretation;
- a **code of practice** is a voluntary route to showing compliance;
- a **harmonised standard**, once its reference is in the Official Journal, gives a **presumption of conformity** under Article 40.

As amended, Article 50(7) lets the Commission assess a code's adequacy and adopt common rules by implementing act if a code proves inadequate.
term:Code of Practice on Marking and Lab.exam_tip: The Code of Practice on Marking and Labelling is voluntary, final 10 June 2026, under Article 50(7): Section 1 provider marking, Section 2 deployer labelling. A code demonstrates compliance; only a harmonised standard gives a presumption of conformity.

term:Product Liability Directive (EU) 20.deep_dive:
The revised Product Liability Directive was adopted on 23 October 2024, published in the Official Journal on 18 November 2024 and entered into force on 8 December 2024. Member States must transpose it by **9 December 2026**, and it applies to products placed on the market or put into service after that date. From 9 December 2026 it repeals Directive 85/374/EEC, which still governs products placed on the market earlier.

Three features matter most for AI:

- **Software is a product.** Article 4(1) covers all movables including software, however supplied: on a device, through a network, or as software-as-a-service (recital 13). Free and open-source software supplied outside a commercial activity is excluded (Article 2(2)), but a manufacturer that integrates it into its own product is liable for it.
- **No-fault liability.** The claimant proves defect, damage and causation (Article 10(1)). Damage includes death or personal injury, medically recognised psychological harm, property damage, and destruction or corruption of non-professional data (Article 6).
- **Aids to the claimant.** Once the claim is plausible, the court can order disclosure of evidence (Article 9). Defect is presumed where the defendant fails to disclose, the product breaches mandatory safety requirements, or there is an obvious malfunction; causation is presumed where the damage is typical of the defect. Where technical or scientific complexity makes proof excessively difficult, both can be presumed, and machine learning is named as an example (Article 10, recital 48).

The defect test weighs continued learning after placement (Article 7), and a substantial modification through an update counts as a fresh placing on the market (recital 40). Maximum harmonisation means Member States cannot set stricter or looser rules.
term:Product Liability Directive (EU) 20.exam_tip: PLD (EU) 2024/2853: transposition by 9 December 2026, applying to products placed on the market after that date, repealing Directive 85/374/EEC. No-fault; software including AI is a product however supplied; the presumptions of defect and causation are rebuttable.

term:Product Liability.deep_dive:
Product liability is the body of law that holds manufacturers and sellers responsible for harm caused by defective products. It reaches AI through three theories:

| Theory | What it covers |
|---|---|
| **Design defect** | The product was made as intended but the design is unreasonably dangerous |
| **Manufacturing defect** | The product departs from the intended design |
| **Failure to warn** (marketing defect) | Instructions or warnings are inadequate |

These run through three standards: **strict liability** (prove the product was defective and caused harm, no negligence needed), **negligence** (prove a failure of reasonable care), and **breach of warranty**. Design cases usually turn on a **risk-utility test**: was the risk of harm outweighed by the product's utility, and could a reasonable alternative design have reduced it?

AI complicates each step. Behaviour is dynamic and context-sensitive, models drift after deployment, and outputs are probabilistic. The 2018 Uber autonomous-vehicle fatality shows the puzzle: was the defect in the algorithm, the sensor configuration, or the testing protocol? In the United States, whether software is a 'product' is still argued state by state, and a mid-2025 jury verdict in the Tesla Autopilot litigation awarded more than **USD 240 million** for a 2019 death. The EU settled the software question by statute: under the revised Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853, software including AI systems is a product however it is supplied.
term:Product Liability.exam_tip: Know the three theories (design, manufacturing, failure to warn) and the three standards (strict liability, negligence, warranty). Design claims turn on the risk-utility test and a reasonable alternative design. The EU PLD settles that software is a product.

term:AI Liability Directive (Withdrawn).deep_dive:
The AI Liability Directive was the Commission's proposed companion to the revised Product Liability Directive. Proposed on **28 September 2022** (COM(2022) 496), it was fault-based and aimed at national tort claims, not defective products. Its two headline devices would have been:

- a power for national courts to order disclosure of evidence about high-risk AI systems suspected of causing damage; and
- a rebuttable **presumption of causality** linking a fault to the damage, easing the victim's burden of proof.

It never became law. Work was suspended until the AI Act was adopted and resumed in 2024, but the Parliament's internal market committee called the proposal premature and unnecessary in May 2025. The Commission announced the withdrawal in its **2025 work programme** (COM(2025) 45, 11 February 2025), approved it on 16 July 2025, and published the withdrawal in the Official Journal as **OJ C/2025/5423 on 6 October 2025**. The 2026 Digital Omnibus on AI added no liability rules.

The consequence is the fact most likely to be tested: as of 2026 there is **no EU-level fault-based AI liability regime**. Victims rely on the revised Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853 for defective products and on national tort law for fault. An answer that cites an 'AI Liability Directive presumption' is wrong.
term:AI Liability Directive (Withdrawn).exam_tip: The AI Liability Directive was proposed 28 September 2022 and withdrawn (OJ C/2025/5423, 6 October 2025). It never applied. Do not cite its disclosure or causality presumption as law; the PLD and national tort law fill the gap.

term:ISO/IEC 42006.deep_dive:
ISO/IEC 42006:2025, published on **7 July 2025**, sets requirements for the bodies that audit and certify AI management systems against ISO/IEC 42001. It adds AI-specific requirements on top of **ISO/IEC 17021-1**, the general standard for bodies that audit and certify management systems. In other words, it governs the **certifiers**, not the organizations being certified.

That is the whole point of the term, and the distinction the exam tests. Three standards get confused:

| Standard | Who it binds | Certifiable? |
|---|---|---|
| **ISO/IEC 42001** | The organization's AI management system (AIMS) | Yes: the AIMS is certified |
| **ISO/IEC 42005** | Guidance on AI system impact assessment | No: guidance only |
| **ISO/IEC 42006** | The certification body that audits a 42001 AIMS | The certifier is accredited, not certified to 42006 |

So a company seeking a 42001 certificate is audited by a body that must itself meet 42006. A 42005 impact assessment is never certified; it is one well-regarded way to satisfy 42001's impact-assessment clauses (6.1.4 and 8.4, and Annex A objective A.5), and the 42001 auditor tests those clauses, not the 42005 standard.

Like 42005, 42006 is part of the ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 42 AI family and rests on the shared ISO/IEC 22989 vocabulary.
term:ISO/IEC 42006.exam_tip: ISO/IEC 42006:2025 (7 July 2025) sets requirements for the bodies that audit and certify a 42001 AIMS, building on ISO/IEC 17021-1. It binds the certifier, not the certified organization.

term:ISO/IEC 42005.deep_dive:
ISO/IEC 42005:2025, published on **28 May 2025** (first edition, 39 pages, ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 42), is guidance on AI system impact assessment. It tells an organization how to set up and run a repeatable process for assessing how an AI system, and the ways it can foreseeably be used, may affect individuals, groups of individuals and society.

Two clauses carry the structure:

- **Clause 5** is the process: document it, integrate it with other management processes, set the timing, define the scope, allocate responsibilities, set thresholds for sensitive and restricted uses and impact scales, perform, analyse, record and report, approve, and monitor and review.
- **Clause 6** is what one assessment records: scope; system information (description, capabilities, purpose, intended and unintended uses); data and data quality; algorithms and models; the deployment environment; interested parties; actual and reasonably foreseeable benefits and harms including failures and misuse; and the measures chosen.

Five informative annexes: A for use with 42001, B for use with 23894, C a harms-and-benefits taxonomy, D aligning with other assessments, and E an example template.

Three facts the exam returns to. It is **guidance and cannot be certified**. It is for any organization that develops, provides or uses AI, so a deployer cannot simply rely on its vendor. And it is **two-sided**: a record with harms but no benefits, or no unintended uses, is incomplete. It is one of BOK v2.1's three core ISO standards, with 22989 and 42001.
term:ISO/IEC 42005.exam_tip: 42001 requires the assessment; 42005 explains how and is never certified. Change of intended use is the classic reassessment trigger, and 42001 clause 8.4 adds planned intervals and proposed significant changes. A 42005 record can feed a DPIA or FRIA but never replaces either.

term:Notice.deep_dive:
Notice is the duty to tell people how their personal data will be collected, used, stored and shared. GDPR Article 13 covers data collected directly from the person; Article 14 covers data obtained elsewhere. The required content is fixed: controller and DPO identity, purposes, legal basis, any legitimate interest, recipients, transfers, retention, data subject rights, and the automated-decision disclosure.

For AI the load-bearing clause is Article 13(2)(f), mirrored by Article 15(1)(h): where automated decision-making or profiling happens, the controller must give meaningful information about the logic involved, plus the significance and envisaged consequences. The CJEU settled the standard in Dun & Bradstreet Austria (C-203/22, 27 February 2025): a concise, intelligible account of the procedure and principles actually applied to that person, not a formula dump. Telling the person how a change in their inputs would have changed the result may be enough.

Article 14 is the one that catches generative AI. A model trained on web-scraped data processes personal data not obtained from the subject, so notice is owed. Developers often invoke the Article 14(5)(b) disproportionate-effort exception, but it requires safeguards, including publishing the information. The EDPB's draft web-scraping guidelines (03/2026, consultation to 30 October 2026) treat individual notices as often impossible or disproportionate, while still demanding transparency by design.

AI-specific notice failures: opaque logic, inference that creates sensitive facts from ordinary inputs, models whose behaviour shifts after collection, and provenance that cannot be traced.
term:Notice.exam_tip: Two articles, two triggers: Article 13 for data you collect directly, Article 14 for scraped or third-party data. The AI hook is Article 13(2)(f), and Dun & Bradstreet defines what 'meaningful information about the logic' actually means.

term:Consent.deep_dive:
Consent is one of six GDPR Article 6 lawful bases, defined in Article 4(11) as a freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication of the data subject's wishes, given by a statement or clear affirmative action. Article 7 adds the conditions: the controller must be able to demonstrate consent, the request must be in clear plain language and separable from other matters, and consent can be withdrawn at any time as easily as it was given. For special-category data, Article 9(2)(a) sets a higher bar: explicit consent.

Two exam points are easy to miss. First, there is no hierarchy among the six bases, and consent is not the default; the controller picks a basis and justifies it. Second, consent is a poor fit for AI training at scale. The EDPB's draft Guidelines 03/2026 say consent would most probably not be workable for large-scale web scraping, which is why developers usually rely on legitimate interest instead.

AI erodes the four validity elements. Power imbalance: people cannot refuse an AI embedded in an essential service. Lack of understanding: nobody grasps what a deep model will infer. Opacity: hidden or undocumented uses. Dark patterns: pre-ticked boxes, bundled services, hidden opt-outs and biased defaults, all of which fail the informed and specific tests.

Bundled consent, pre-checked boxes and implicit consent generally fail for AI. Opt-in is the GDPR default; opt-out exists only in limited jurisdictions.
term:Consent.exam_tip: Implied consent fails: continued use, silence and pre-ticked boxes are not an affirmative act (Recital 32), and a power imbalance (employer, public body) undermines 'freely given'. Withdrawal does not make earlier processing unlawful (Art. 7(3)), but with no other basis it is an Art. 17 erasure ground.

term:Choice.deep_dive:
Choice is the broader control that sits around consent: the options a person has about whether and how their data is collected and used. In the GDPR, choice shows up in three places. Article 21 gives the right to object, including to profiling. Article 22 gives the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing with legal or similarly significant effects, and Article 22(3) adds safeguards where an exception applies: human intervention, the right to express a point of view, and the right to contest the decision. Article 7(3) allows withdrawal of consent.

The default matters. GDPR is an opt-in regime: consent requires a clear affirmative act. The US model inverts it. Under the California Consumer Privacy Act and CPRA, choice is mainly opt-out: the right to opt out of sale or sharing, and, under the CPPA's automated decision-making technology regulations, rights to opt out of ADMT, to access information about it, and to have a human review certain decisions.

Choice is only real if it is usable. Dark patterns defeat it: forced consent through bundled services, obscured opt-out buttons, biased defaults, and the illusion of choice where every option leads to the same outcome. GDPR Article 25(2) pushes the other way with data protection by default, so the privacy-protective setting must be the starting point rather than something the user must find.

Article 22 is narrower than it looks. It reaches decisions based solely on automated processing, and meaningful human involvement can take a decision outside it, but the human review must be genuine, not a rubber stamp.
term:Choice.exam_tip: Opt-in is the GDPR default and opt-out is the CCPA and CPRA model. Keep Article 21 (objection) distinct from Article 22 (solely automated decisions), and remember Article 22(3) safeguards: intervene, express a view, contest.

term:Privacy by Design.deep_dive:
Privacy by design is the architectural rule that privacy is built in from the start, not bolted on. It was formulated by Ann Cavoukian in the 1990s and given legal force by GDPR Article 25, which has two halves. Article 25(1), by design, requires appropriate technical and organisational measures, such as pseudonymisation, implemented both when the means of processing are determined and during processing itself, weighing the state of the art, cost, the nature and context of processing, and the risks to individuals. Article 25(2), by default, requires that only the personal data necessary for each purpose is processed, and that defaults do not make data accessible to an indefinite number of people without the person acting.

Cavoukian's seven principles are examinable: proactive not reactive; privacy as the default; privacy embedded into design; full functionality (a positive-sum, not privacy versus utility); end-to-end security across the lifecycle; visibility and transparency; and respect for the user.

Applied to AI, the lifecycle mapping is concrete. At problem framing: a DPIA and a necessity and proportionality test. During data and model work: privacy-preserving training such as federated learning and differential privacy, bias detection, and interpretability tooling. In operation: limited retention of raw inputs, contestability, and drift monitoring. In MLOps the controls become engineering practice: privacy scans in CI/CD, privacy linting, model cards that record privacy characteristics, and drift detection that flags new risks from divergence between training and live data.
term:Privacy by Design.exam_tip: Article 25 has two halves: by design (measures at the time you choose the means and while processing) and by default (only necessary data, privacy-protective settings). Know Cavoukian's seven principles, including full functionality, the positive-sum idea.

term:Federated Learning.deep_dive:
Federated learning trains a model across decentralised devices or clients and shares only model updates, never the raw data. Each client computes a local update on data it holds, and an aggregator combines the updates into a global model. For AI governance this is a design measure: it fits GDPR Article 25 by design and the minimisation principle in Article 5(1)(c), because raw personal data is never centralised.

It is not a privacy silver bullet, and the exam expects you to know that. Shared updates can leak information about the local data they were computed from, through gradient inversion or membership inference. The standard hardening is to pair federated learning with differential privacy, secure aggregation, or encryption, so the aggregator never sees an individual client's contribution in the clear.

Federated learning also complicates erasure. Article 17 requires deletion on request, but pulling one client's contribution out of an already-trained global model means retraining or model editing, and the distributed update history makes that harder, not easier. This is why the EDPB Opinion 28/2024 anonymity test is applied to the resulting model, not to the raw data: if it is not insignificantly likely that a training subject's data could be extracted directly or through queries, the model still processes personal data and the GDPR duties follow it.
term:Federated Learning.exam_tip: Federated learning shares model updates, not raw data, which is why it is a minimisation and Article 25 measure. It is not anonymisation: updates can leak, so it is paired with differential privacy or secure aggregation, and it makes Article 17 erasure harder.

term:Differential Privacy.deep_dive:
Differential privacy is a mathematical guarantee, not a technique. It adds calibrated noise to outputs so that including or excluding any single record changes the distribution of results by at most a bounded factor. That factor is the privacy budget, epsilon. The trade-off is exact and examinable: a smaller epsilon means stronger privacy and less utility; a larger epsilon means more accurate results and weaker protection.

The two settings are local differential privacy, where noise is added on the device before data leaves it, and central differential privacy, where a trusted aggregator adds noise to the combined result. Local protects against the aggregator, central gives better utility.

Where it sits in the GDPR. Differential privacy is a technical measure under Article 25 by design and supports the minimisation principle in Article 5(1)(c). EDPB Opinion 28/2024 lists it among the methods that reduce identifiability in training, alongside regularisation against overfitting, and among the output-side measures that help resist membership inference, extraction and regurgitation. At training time it limits the influence of any one data point, which also eases Article 17 erasure, because forgetting a record matters less when its effect was bounded from the start.

One caution: differential privacy is not anonymisation on its own. It bounds inference risk; it does not by itself make a dataset or a model non-personal data, and the guarantee is only as good as the epsilon chosen and the mechanism implemented.
term:Differential Privacy.exam_tip: Epsilon is the exam hook: lower means more privacy, less utility. Treat differential privacy as a minimisation safeguard under Article 25, not as automatic anonymisation, and remember Opinion 28/2024 names it as an identifiability-reducing technique.

term:OECD Framework for the Classificati.deep_dive:
Published in February 2022 as OECD Digital Economy Papers No. 323, and built by the OECD.AI Network of Experts (ONE AI), this framework lets policy makers, regulators and governance teams characterise an AI system in context and connect its technical features to the policy concerns in the OECD AI Principles.

It has five dimensions. People & Planet covers who interacts with or is affected by the system, including users and their competence, impacted stakeholders, optionality and redress, human rights, well-being and the environment. Economic Context covers the sector and setting: industrial sector, business function and model, criticality, breadth of deployment and technical maturity. Data & Input covers detection and collection, provenance, dynamic or static data, rights and identifiability, structure, scale and quality. AI Model covers model type, open or proprietary, generative or discriminative, how it is built, whether it evolves in the field, central or federated, and its transparency. Task & Output covers the tasks performed, composite systems, action autonomy, core application area and evaluation methods.

The framework is used to build registries and inventories of algorithms and automated decision systems, to support sector frameworks in health and finance, to structure risk assessment, to give a common basis for reporting AI incidents, and to guide risk management across the lifecycle.

Two framing points. In the lab, meaning conception and development before deployment, only Data & Input, AI Model and Task & Output apply, which suits ex ante risk management. In the field, after deployment, all five apply, which suits ex post management. The dimensions also map to lifecycle stages so you can see which AI actors are responsible at each point.
term:OECD Framework for the Classificati.exam_tip: Expect 'which dimension holds this criterion' questions. Action autonomy sits under Task & Output, not AI Model; opt-out and redress under People & Planet; sector, criticality and scale under Economic Context. Lab uses three dimensions, field uses all five.

term:OECD AI System Definition (2023 Upd.deep_dive:
The OECD Council adopted the revised definition on 8 November 2023, after the Digital Policy Committee approved the draft with the Working Party on AI Governance on 16 October 2023. An explanatory memorandum followed in March 2024 as OECD AI Papers No. 8.

The wording: an AI system is a machine-based system that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers from the input it receives how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments. Systems vary in their levels of autonomy and adaptiveness after deployment.

Five edits separate it from the 2019 text, and each has one job. Explicit or implicit objectives captures goals that are learned rather than programmed, for example through reinforcement learning from human feedback. Inferring from the input explains how outputs arise. Adding content brings generative AI inside the definition. Physical replacing real is a clarity fix, not a scope change, because virtual environments are real too. Adaptiveness after deployment covers systems such as recommenders that keep evolving in use.

Why it matters beyond the OECD. The EU AI Act's Article 3(1) definition closely tracks this wording, and Recital 12 calls for the notion of an AI system to be aligned with the work of international organisations. The update was timed to support that alignment. NIST's AI RMF also borrows OECD vocabulary, including its framing of AI Actors. For the exam, the definition is the common thread that lets one system be recognised across the OECD, the AI Act and the NIST framework.
term:OECD AI System Definition (2023 Upd.exam_tip: Match each edit to its single purpose: content equals generative AI, explicit or implicit equals learned goals, physical is wording clarity not a scope change, adaptiveness equals post-deployment learning. The EU AI Act Article 3(1) definition tracks the OECD wording.

term:OECD AI Principles.deep_dive:
The Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence, OECD/LEGAL/0449, is the first intergovernmental standard on AI. It was adopted on 22 May 2019 and revised twice: on 8 November 2023, which changed only the AI system definition, and on 3 May 2024, which made substantive updates. It is non-binding, a political commitment, and had 47 adherents in September 2026, the European Union among them.

It has two sections: five value-based principles and five national policy recommendations. The five principles, by their 2024 headings, are inclusive growth, sustainable development and well-being; respect for the rule of law, human rights and democratic values, including fairness and privacy; transparency and explainability; robustness, security and safety; and accountability. The five policy recommendations cover investment in AI research and development, an inclusive AI-enabling ecosystem, an interoperable governance and policy environment, human capacity and labour market transition, and international co-operation.

The 2024 revision added information integrity, explicit coverage of misuse including uses outside the intended purpose, safe override, repair and decommissioning mechanisms, responsible business conduct, interoperable governance and environmental sustainability. It also moved traceability and systematic risk management into the Accountability principle, and expanded the heading of Principle 1.2, which was previously human-centred values and fairness.

Reach matters. The G20 AI Principles welcomed at the 2019 Osaka summit were drawn directly from the OECD Recommendation, which gave the principles global traction beyond OECD membership.
term:OECD AI Principles.exam_tip: Know the five principles by their 2024 headings, and keep the two revision dates straight: 8 November 2023 changed only the definition, 3 May 2024 changed the substance. Principle 1.2 is now about the rule of law, human rights and democratic values, including fairness and privacy.

term:OECD AI Incidents and Hazards Monit.deep_dive:
The AI Incidents and Hazards Monitor is an OECD.AI tool that tracks AI incidents and hazards reported in the news. It automatically classifies articles against the OECD's incident and hazard definitions, giving policy makers and governance teams a running view of what is being reported, by sector and by harm type.

Its most examinable feature is its limitation. Because it depends on public reporting, it captures only a subset of the incidents that actually occur. Absence from AIM is not evidence that nothing happened; it means nothing was reported and picked up. Reporting bias, language bias and news attention all shape what appears.

AIM sits alongside a second OECD instrument: the common reporting framework for AI incidents (OECD AI Papers No. 34, February 2025), a shared set of reporting criteria so that jurisdictions can report consistently while keeping their own rules. The two together are the OECD's incident infrastructure, distinct from its hazard and incident definitions themselves.

Used well, AIM is an external-environment input. It feeds the context analysis and risk identification an organisation does when it scans for foreseeable harm, and it shows which harm patterns are emerging in its sector. Used badly, it becomes a false assurance that the AI incident rate is low because the feed is quiet.
term:OECD AI Incidents and Hazards Monit.exam_tip: AIM tracks publicly reported events only, so it is a subset, not a census. Remember the companion piece: the OECD common reporting framework for AI incidents, AI Papers No. 34, February 2025.

term:Hiroshima AI Process Reporting Fram.deep_dive:
The Hiroshima AI Process reporting framework is a voluntary, common format through which organisations report how they align with the G7 Hiroshima Process International Code of Conduct for Organisations Developing Advanced AI Systems. The Code came out of Japan's 2023 G7 presidency and was advanced under Italy's 2024 presidency. The OECD hosts the framework and publishes the reports on OECD.AI.

The division of labour is the exam point: the G7 wrote the Code, the OECD runs the reporting. The framework launched in February 2025. Its first round drew 25 organisations, which the OECD analysed in How are AI developers managing risks?. Version 2.0 widens participation beyond developers to organisations deploying and providing advanced AI systems. Submissions received by 30 September 2026 feed the next analytical review.

Legal effect: none. It is a transparency and comparability tool, not a certification or an enforcement regime. That separates it from the EU's GPAI Code of Practice, which providers can use to demonstrate compliance with the AI Act. The Hiroshima framework asks organisations to describe their risk management practices in a shared vocabulary so that regulators, researchers and the public can compare them.

For an AI governance professional, it is an external accountability option: a way to publish how the organisation manages frontier-model risks, in a format that other organisations and governments already use.
term:Hiroshima AI Process Reporting Fram.exam_tip: The G7 wrote the Code of Conduct; the OECD runs the reporting, launched February 2025. It is voluntary with no legal effect, unlike the EU GPAI Code of Practice, which is tied to AI Act compliance.

term:AI Incident vs. AI Hazard (OECD Def.deep_dive:
The OECD set these definitions in Defining AI incidents and related terms, OECD AI Papers No. 16, May 2024. An AI incident is an event, circumstance or series of events where the development, use or malfunction of one or more AI systems directly or indirectly leads to harm. An AI hazard is an event, circumstance or series of events that could plausibly lead to an incident. Near misses count as hazards: no harm occurred, but it plausibly could have.

Four harm types apply to incidents and hazards alike: injury or harm to the health of people; disruption of the management and operation of critical infrastructure; violations of human rights or breaches of legal obligations protecting fundamental, labour and intellectual property rights; and harm to property, communities or the environment, under which reputational and financial harm to organisations counts as harm to property.

The tiers nest. A serious AI incident is one where the harm is serious: death or serious harm to health, serious and irreversible disruption of critical infrastructure, serious violation of rights, or serious harm to property, communities or the environment. An AI disaster is a serious incident that disrupts the functioning of a community or society and may test or exceed its capacity to cope with its own resources. A serious AI hazard is an event that could plausibly lead to a serious incident or a disaster. The serious-incident wording was drafted to align with the definition proposed in the EU AI Act context.

An event can include interactions between AI systems, including agentic ones, and AI-related risks count as hazards to the extent they could lead to incidents.
term:AI Incident vs. AI Hazard (OECD Def.exam_tip: Did harm happen: incident. Could it plausibly have happened, including a caught error: hazard. Was the harm serious: serious incident. Did it overwhelm a community's ability to cope: AI disaster. Near misses are hazards, and the tiers nest.

term:ISO/IEC 42001.deep_dive:
ISO/IEC 42001:2023 was published in December 2023 by ISO and IEC through JTC 1. It is the first international certifiable AI management system standard, the AI analogue of ISO/IEC 27001 for information security. It is a requirements standard: it specifies what must be done, not how, so organisations choose their own implementation methods.

Scope is any organisation, regardless of size, sector or AI maturity. Structure follows Annex SL, Clauses 4 to 10: Context of the organization, Leadership, Planning, Support, Operation, Performance evaluation and Improvement. Annex A holds the normative controls, which an organisation must implement or justify excluding; Annex B gives informative implementation guidance; Annex C links to responsible AI objectives and ethical principles.

Three planning activities are mandatory: risk assessment (Clause 6.1.2), risk treatment (Clause 6.1.3) and impact assessment (Clause 6.1.4). Thirteen categories of documented information are required for certification. The AIMS is organisation-scoped, so two organisations running the same AI system can hold different AIMS and different certificates.

Certification is by third-party accredited bodies, and the certifiers are governed by ISO/IEC 42006, published 7 July 2025, which sets requirements additional to ISO/IEC 17021-1. 42006 governs the certifiers, not the certified. The standard sits in an ecosystem: ISO/IEC 22989 for terminology, ISO/IEC 23894 for AI risk management and ISO/IEC 42005 for impact assessment guidance.
term:ISO/IEC 42001.exam_tip: The AIMS is what gets certified, scoped to the organization, so two companies using the same model can hold different certificates. Annex A exclusions need justification in the statement of applicability. ISO/IEC 42006 governs the certification bodies, not the organizations.

term:Context of the Organization.deep_dive:
Context of the Organization is Clause 4 of ISO/IEC 42001, and it is the first auditable clause. Its purpose is to make the organisation understand why AI matters to it before it plans anything. The requirements are to analyse the external and internal factors that affect the AIMS and its performance, to identify interested parties and their needs and expectations, using the stakeholder vocabulary of ISO/IEC 22989, and to define and document the scope of the AIMS, including what is in, what is out and where the boundaries lie (Clause 4.3).

Three dimensions of context carry the work. The competitive and stakeholder dimension covers industry analysis, customer trends and how AI reshapes market segments. The legal dimension covers the laws that apply, such as the GDPR, the EU AI Act, US instruments including NYC Local Law 144 and EEOC guidance on algorithmic discrimination, and sector-specific rules. The ethical dimension covers responsible AI principles.

Context is not a document you write and file. It is the input to planning: the risks identified under Clause 6.1, the objectives under Clause 6.2 and the impact assessment under Clause 6.1.4 must trace back to it. Auditors test two things in particular: whether the context analysis is fresh rather than recycled from an old information-security or quality project, and whether there is a visible thread from context to planning to operation to improvement.

Getting it wrong at Clause 4 propagates. A thin context produces a generic AI policy, a risk register that misses the real exposures and an impact assessment that no one trusts.
term:Context of the Organization.exam_tip: Role determination in 4.1 is the AI-specific step: one organization can be a provider for one system and a customer for another, and the role shapes which controls apply. Auditor evidence for Clause 4: an analysis of internal and external issues and interested-party needs, plus the documented scope (4.3).

term:Annex SL.deep_dive:
Annex SL is ISO's harmonised structure for management system standards, now carried in the ISO/IEC Directives as the Harmonized Structure. It gives every modern management system standard the same skeleton, so organisations can integrate them rather than run parallel systems.

The shared clauses are 4 to 10: Context of the organization, Leadership, Planning, Support, Operation, Performance evaluation and Improvement. Annex SL also fixes common terms and core text, so the same concepts carry the same meaning across standards. ISO/IEC 42001, ISO 9001 for quality, ISO/IEC 27001 for information security, ISO 14001 for environment and ISO 45001 for occupational health and safety all follow it.

The practical consequences are what the exam tests. One integrated management system can hold a single AI policy, a shared documented-information regime under Clause 7.5, and one internal audit programme that covers several standards at once. An organisation already certified to ISO/IEC 27001 starts from a familiar structure when it builds an AIMS, which is why 42001 is often described as integrable with 27001 rather than competing with it.

A structural point worth remembering: Clauses 1 to 3 are informational (scope, normative references, terms and definitions), and Clauses 4 to 10 contain the auditable requirements. When a question asks which clause a requirement sits in, that split is usually the first filter.
term:Annex SL.exam_tip: Shared clauses are why a 27001-certified organization can extend its management system to 42001 instead of building a parallel one. An internal audit finding belongs to Check (Clause 9); correcting the nonconformity and its root cause is Act (Clause 10).

term:Intended Purpose (Art. 3(12)).deep_dive:
### Definition
The intended purpose is the use the provider designs the system for, including the specific context and conditions of use. It is read from what the provider itself says: instructions for use, promotional and sales material, statements, and technical documentation.

### What hangs on it
- **Classification.** Annex III lists systems by use, so the same model can be high-risk in hiring and minimal risk when drafting emails. Adding human oversight does not lower the tier; oversight is itself a high-risk requirement.
- **Data.** Art. 10(3) judges training, validation and test data in view of the intended purpose.
- **Role shifts.** A deployer or other third party that changes the intended purpose of a non-high-risk system so that it becomes high-risk is treated as its provider (Art. 25(1)(c)).

### Reasonably foreseeable misuse (Art. 3(13))
Use that departs from the intended purpose but can result from predictable human behaviour or from interaction with other systems, including other AI systems. Art. 9 requires high-risk providers to estimate and evaluate risks both under intended use and under reasonably foreseeable misuse, and the instructions for use must flag known or foreseeable circumstances of either kind that may lead to risks (Art. 13(3)). Providers therefore design, warn or document against misuse they can predict.
term:Intended Purpose (Art. 3(12)).exam_tip: Classification follows intended purpose and context, never the technique or the mitigations. Foreseeable misuse belongs in the provider's risk management, and a deployer that changes the purpose into a high-risk use becomes the provider.

term:Substantial Modification (Art. 3(23.deep_dive:
### The test
A change is a substantial modification when all of these hold: it happens after the system is placed on the market or put into service; the provider did not foresee or plan it in the initial conformity assessment; and it either affects compliance with the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements (Arts. 8-15) or changes the intended purpose the system was assessed for.

### Consequences
- **New conformity assessment (Art. 43(4)):** required whether the modified system will be distributed further or stays with the current deployer.
- **Role shift (Art. 25(1)(b)):** a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party that substantially modifies a high-risk system, leaving it high-risk, becomes its provider.
- **Legacy systems (Art. 111(2)):** high-risk systems on the market before their category's high-risk date come under the rules only if their design later changes significantly. Recital 177 says 'significant change' means the same in substance as substantial modification.

### Continuous learning
For systems that keep learning after release, changes the provider pre-determined at the initial conformity assessment, and recorded in the technical documentation (Annex IV point 2(f)), are not substantial modifications. A provider of a learning system should therefore define the planned scope of change before release.
term:Substantial Modification (Art. 3(23.exam_tip: Unplanned change plus an effect on compliance or intended purpose equals a substantial modification: a new conformity assessment, and a new provider if a third party made the change. Changes pre-determined in the original assessment do not count, and a legacy system stays outside the rules until such a change.

term:Value Chain Responsibilities (Art..deep_dive:
### The three triggers (Art. 25(1))
A distributor, importer, deployer or other third party becomes the provider, with all Art. 16 duties, when it:
1. puts its own name or trademark on a high-risk system already on the market, unless a contract allocates the obligations otherwise;
2. makes a substantial modification to a high-risk system that leaves it high-risk;
3. changes the intended purpose of a system that was not high-risk, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk.

### The original provider (Art. 25(2))
It stops being the provider of that system but must cooperate with the new one. As amended by the 2026 Omnibus, that means technical documentation, known limitations and failure modes, and targeted access for testing. The duty falls away only if it clearly specified that its system must not be turned into a high-risk system.

### Related rules
- **Product manufacturers (Art. 25(3)):** one shipping a high-risk AI safety component in an Annex I Section A product under its own name is the provider.
- **Suppliers (Art. 25(4)):** a high-risk provider and its suppliers of components, tools or models agree in writing on information and access; open-source suppliers are exempt unless they supply a general-purpose AI model.

An employer configuring a general-purpose agent platform to reject job applicants is a trigger 3 case.
term:Value Chain Responsibilities (Art..exam_tip: Rebrand, substantially modify, or repurpose into a high-risk use: each makes you the provider with full Art. 16 duties. Trigger 3 is the one candidates miss, because the starting system was not high-risk at all.

term:Emotion Recognition Ban (Art. 5(1)(.deep_dive:
### Scope of the ban
Art. 5(1)(f) bans placing on the market, putting into service for this purpose, or using AI to infer the emotions of people in the workplace or in education institutions. The Commission's 2025 guidelines read both settings broadly: 'workplace' covers candidates in recruitment and employees on probation, and 'education institutions' covers candidates in admission. A call centre tracking its own agents' anger is banned; tracking its customers' anger is not. The exception covers systems put in place for medical or safety reasons, such as therapeutic tools. Recital 44 explains the ban: the science is shaky because emotional expression varies across cultures, situations and individuals, and the power imbalance at work and school makes harm likely.

### What counts as emotion recognition
Art. 3(39) requires inference of emotions or intentions from biometric data such as face, voice or physiological signals. Recital 18 excludes physical states like pain or fatigue, so a system detecting a pilot's or driver's fatigue is outside, as is detecting a smile or a raised voice without inferring an emotion.

### Outside work and school
Emotion recognition is permitted but high-risk under Annex III point 1(c), and deployers must tell people exposed to it (Art. 50(3)).
term:Emotion Recognition Ban (Art. 5(1)(.exam_tip: Employees, job candidates and students: banned unless the purpose is medical or safety. Customers and shoppers: allowed, but high-risk with an Art. 50(3) notice. Fatigue detection and text-only sentiment analysis are not emotion recognition under the Act.

term:Real-Time Remote Biometric Identifi.deep_dive:
### Conditions on every permitted use
- **Purpose (Art. 5(2)):** only to confirm the identity of the specifically targeted person, weighing the harm if the system is not used against the consequences for everyone's rights.
- **Before use:** the police authority must complete a fundamental rights impact assessment (Art. 27) and register the system in the EU database; in urgent cases registration may follow without undue delay.
- **Authorisation (Art. 5(3)):** each use needs prior approval from a judicial authority or an independent administrative authority whose decision binds. In a justified emergency use may start first, but authorisation must be requested within 24 hours; if refused, use stops and all data and outputs are deleted. No decision with adverse legal effect may rest solely on the system's output.
- **Notification (Art. 5(4)):** each use is notified to the market surveillance authority and the national data protection authority.
- **National opt-in (Art. 5(5)):** the exceptions work only where a Member State's law allows them, and states may adopt stricter rules.

### Boundaries
National security uses fall outside the Act altogether (Art. 2(3)). Real-time identification by private parties, or by police outside publicly accessible spaces, is not caught by this ban; where lawful it is high-risk under Annex III point 1(a), and GDPR Art. 9 still governs non-police biometric processing.

term:Remote Biometric Identification (RB.deep_dive:
### Three things to tell apart
- **Identification (one-to-many):** who is this person? The system compares a captured face or voice with many stored templates. Remote identification happens without the person's active involvement, as with cameras in a station.
- **Verification (one-to-one, Art. 3(36)):** is this person who they claim to be? Unlocking a phone, or an e-gate checking a traveller against their own passport. Annex III point 1(a) excludes verification whose sole purpose is confirming a claimed identity.
- **Categorisation (Art. 3(40)):** sorting people into groups from biometric data, regulated separately.

### Real-time versus post
Real-time (Art. 3(42)) means capture, comparison and identification happen without significant delay; limited short delays still count, to stop circumvention. Post (Art. 3(43)) is everything else, such as running stored CCTV footage against a database after an incident.

### Where each lands
- Real-time, law enforcement, publicly accessible spaces: prohibited unless an Art. 5(1)(h) exception applies.
- Other real-time uses and all post-event uses: high-risk under Annex III point 1(a), where Union or national law permits them.
- Police using post-event identification in a targeted search for a suspect must seek judicial or binding administrative authorisation beforehand or within 48 hours (Art. 26(10)), and may never use it untargeted.
term:Remote Biometric Identification (RB.exam_tip: Real-time plus law enforcement plus public space is the only RBI combination Art. 5 bans. Post-event identification is high-risk (48-hour authorisation for police), and 1:1 verification such as a phone unlock falls outside Annex III point 1(a).

term:Social Scoring Ban (Art. 5(1)(c)).deep_dive:
### The elements
1. Evaluating or classifying people or groups over a period of time.
2. Based on their social behaviour, or on known, inferred or predicted personal or personality characteristics.
3. The resulting score leads to either or both of: detrimental or unfavourable treatment in social contexts unrelated to where the data was generated or collected; or treatment that is unjustified or disproportionate to the behaviour or its gravity.

### Who it binds
Recital 31 refers to social scoring by public or private actors, and the article names no type of actor. Study material that describes only government social scoring understates the ban.

### What it does not catch
Recital 31 says lawful evaluation carried out for a specific purpose under Union and national law is unaffected. Credit scoring that uses financial data to decide a loan is a high-risk Annex III point 5(b) use. The ban applies when data from one part of life feeds a score that penalises someone in another, for instance a landlord refusing a tenancy because of a score built from social media activity, or when the penalty is out of proportion to the conduct.

Breaches fall in the top fine tier: up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover (Art. 99(3)).
term:Social Scoring Ban (Art. 5(1)(c)).exam_tip: Banned for private and public actors alike. The test is cross-context or disproportionate detrimental treatment; ordinary credit scoring for lending is high-risk under Annex III point 5(b).

term:Predictive Policing Ban (Art. 5(1)(.deep_dive:
### The principle
Recital 42 ties the ban to the presumption of innocence: people should be judged on what they actually do. They should never be judged on AI predictions drawn solely from profiling or traits such as nationality, place of birth or residence, number of children, level of debt or type of car, without reasonable suspicion based on objective verifiable facts and a human assessment of them.

### Three outcomes
- **Banned:** a tool that scores an individual's likelihood of offending purely from a profile or personality traits.
- **High-risk (Annex III point 6(d)):** law-enforcement tools assessing a person's risk of offending or reoffending that are not based solely on profiling, or that assess personality traits or past criminal behaviour. The Art. 5(1)(d) carve-out, AI supporting a human assessment already based on objective, verifiable facts directly linked to a crime, typically lands here.
- **Outside both:** risk analytics that do not profile individuals. Recital 42 gives two examples: flagging likely financial fraud by companies from suspicious transactions, and customs tools predicting where narcotics or illicit goods will be found from known trafficking routes.

### Governance angle
A tool that survives the ban can still entrench bias through feedback loops: patrols sent by earlier predictions generate the records the next model learns from.
term:Predictive Policing Ban (Art. 5(1)(.exam_tip: The key word is 'solely': profiling-only crime prediction about individuals is banned, while tools anchored in objective facts and human assessment are high-risk. Place-based or transaction analytics that profile no person fall outside Art. 5(1)(d).

term:Untargeted Facial Scraping Ban (Art.deep_dive:
### Four conditions, all required
The Commission's 2025 guidelines break the ban into cumulative elements:
- placing on the market, putting into service for this purpose, or use of an AI system, so vendors and users are both exposed;
- the purpose is to create or expand a facial recognition database, meaning any collection that can be used to match faces;
- the database is filled by untargeted scraping, which works like a vacuum cleaner with no focus on particular people;
- the images come from the internet or CCTV footage.

### Boundaries the exam uses
- Honouring robots.txt does not make scraping targeted, and people posting their own photos on social media have not consented to a recognition database.
- Scraping aimed at specific individuals, such as a named suspect or a known group of trafficking victims, is outside the ban. Building a database step by step to reach the same result as untargeted scraping is caught.
- Non-facial biometrics such as voice samples, and scraping without AI, fall outside.
- Harvesting faces to train a model that generates images of fictitious people creates no recognition database, so it is outside; Art. 50 transparency may apply instead.

Recital 43 cites mass surveillance and privacy. Breaches sit in the EUR 35 million or 7% tier (Art. 99(3)).
term:Untargeted Facial Scraping Ban (Art.exam_tip: Building or growing a face-recognition database by scraping the web or CCTV is prohibited outright, so it never reaches the high-risk analysis. Expect the 35 million euro or 7% ceiling as the follow-up, and the fictitious-faces generator as the out-of-scope distractor.

term:Biometric Categorisation Ban (Art..deep_dive:
### The banned practice
Systems that categorise individual people from their biometric data, such as a face or fingerprint, to deduce or infer race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation.

### Carve-out
The ban does not cover lawful labelling, filtering or categorising of biometric datasets acquired under Union or national law. Recital 30 gives the example of sorting images by hair or eye colour, which can be used in law enforcement.

### The rest of biometric categorisation
- Art. 3(40) defines a biometric categorisation system as one that assigns people to categories from biometric data, unless it is ancillary to another commercial service and strictly necessary for objective technical reasons. Recital 16 gives a marketplace filter that previews clothes or glasses on the shopper, and social-network face filters, as ancillary examples.
- Categorisation by sensitive or protected attributes that is not banned is high-risk under Annex III point 1(b).
- Deployers must inform people exposed to a biometric categorisation system (Art. 50(3)).

The GDPR runs in parallel: biometric data processed to uniquely identify a person is special-category data under Art. 9, and the EDPB and supervisory authorities increasingly treat inferred sensitive traits the same way.
term:Biometric Categorisation Ban (Art..exam_tip: Inferring one of the listed sensitive traits from someone's face or body is banned; sorting a lawfully acquired image set is not. Categorisation by other sensitive attributes is high-risk and needs an Art. 50(3) notice.

term:Annex I Product Route (Art. 6(1)).deep_dive:
### The two conditions
Both must be met. A safety component is one that fulfils a safety function or whose failure endangers health, safety or property (Art. 3(14)). The second condition borrows the sector's answer: if a medical device or lift must already go to a notified body, its AI safety component is high-risk under the AI Act. A product the sectoral law lets the maker self-certify does not meet it.

### 2026 Omnibus refinements
- **Art. 6(1a):** AI used solely for non-safety user assistance, performance optimisation, service efficiency, automation, convenience or quality control is not a safety component.
- **Art. 6(1b):** it still counts if its failure would endanger health and safety.
- **Art. 6(1c):** a third-party assessment required only for non-safety risks, such as radio spectrum or electromagnetic interference, does not satisfy the second condition.

### Annex I's two sections
- **Section A:** toys, recreational craft, lifts, equipment for explosive atmospheres, radio equipment, pressure equipment, cableways, personal protective equipment, gas appliances, medical devices and in vitro diagnostics. The high-risk requirements are checked inside the sectoral conformity procedure.
- **Section B:** civil aviation, two- and three-wheel vehicles, agricultural vehicles, motor vehicles, marine equipment and rail, plus machinery since the Omnibus. AI requirements reach them through sectoral acts.

### Dates
2 August 2027 as enacted; 2 August 2028 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.
term:Annex I Product Route (Art. 6(1)).exam_tip: Two-part test: an Annex I product or safety component, and third-party conformity assessment under that product's law. Dates are 2 August 2027 as enacted and 2 August 2028 as amended, separate from the Annex III clock.

term:Annex III High-Risk Areas.deep_dive:
### The eight areas
1. **Biometrics** (where lawful): remote identification, categorisation by sensitive attributes, emotion recognition. Excludes 1:1 verification.
2. **Critical infrastructure:** safety components in critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, and water, gas, heating or electricity supply.
3. **Education:** admission, grading learning outcomes, assessing the level of education a person will receive, and monitoring prohibited behaviour during tests.
4. **Employment:** targeted job ads, CV filtering, candidate evaluation, promotion and termination decisions, task allocation by behaviour or traits, performance monitoring.
5. **Essential services:** public benefits eligibility, creditworthiness and credit scores (except fraud detection), life and health insurance risk pricing, emergency call triage and dispatch.
6. **Law enforcement:** victim risk, polygraphs, evidence reliability, offending risk, profiling in investigations.
7. **Migration, asylum, border control:** polygraphs, risk assessments, application examination, identifying people (except travel-document verification).
8. **Justice and democracy:** helping judges research, interpret and apply the law, and influencing elections or voting (excluding back-office campaign logistics).

### Moving parts
Art. 7 lets the Commission add or modify use cases by delegated act, only inside these eight areas and only for equal or greater risk; it can also remove entries that no longer pose significant risk. Art. 6(3) lets a provider show a listed system is not high-risk.
term:Annex III High-Risk Areas.exam_tip: Most scenario questions are Annex III spotting: CV screening, credit scoring, exam grading and benefits eligibility are high-risk, and a human making the final call does not change that. Fraud detection is the classic carve-out from credit scoring.

term:High-Risk Derogation (Art. 6(3)).deep_dive:
### The filter
Art. 6(3) applies only to systems already listed in Annex III. The question is whether the system materially influences the outcome of decision-making. Recital 53 gives examples for each condition:
- **Narrow procedural task:** turning unstructured data into structured data, sorting incoming documents into categories, detecting duplicates among many applications.
- **Improving a completed human activity:** polishing the tone or style of a document a person already drafted.
- **Detecting decision patterns:** checking after the fact whether a teacher's grading departed from their usual pattern, without replacing or influencing the human assessment absent proper review.
- **Preparatory task:** file handling such as indexing, searching and linking data, or translating initial documents.

### The override
If the system profiles natural persons, in the GDPR Art. 4(4) sense, it is always high-risk, whichever condition it meets.

### The paper trail
The provider must document its assessment before placing the system on the market, register it in the EU database under Art. 49(2), and hand the documentation to authorities on request. As amended by the 2026 Omnibus, registration remains but the summary of grounds and the list of Member States were dropped from Annex VIII Section B. The Commission's Art. 6 guidelines, due 2 February 2026, were published only in draft on 19 May 2026.
term:High-Risk Derogation (Art. 6(3)).exam_tip: Profiling always defeats the derogation. A provider relying on Art. 6(3) still documents its assessment and registers the system in the EU database.

term:High-Risk System Requirements (Arts.deep_dive:
### What Section 2 covers
Articles 8 to 15 set out what a high-risk AI system itself must be like before it reaches the market. Article 8 says the system must meet the requirements that follow, taking account of its intended purpose and the state of the art. The seven substantive articles:

- **Art. 9:** risk management system run across the lifecycle
- **Art. 10:** training, validation and test data that meet quality and governance criteria
- **Art. 11:** technical documentation (Annex IV), drawn up before market placement
- **Art. 12:** automatic event logging
- **Art. 13:** instructions for use and other information for deployers
- **Art. 14:** design for effective human oversight
- **Art. 15:** accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity

### Who carries them
The provider makes the system conform (Art. 16(a)) and proves it through conformity assessment (Art. 43). A harmonised standard cited in the Official Journal creates a presumption of conformity (Art. 40). The QMS (Art. 17) is a Section 3 provider duty; deployers have their own list in Article 26.

### When
As enacted: 2 August 2026 for Annex III systems, 2 August 2027 for Annex I products. As amended by the 2026 Digital Omnibus: 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028.

term:Special-Category Data for Bias Dete.deep_dive:
### Why it exists
Testing a model for discrimination often needs the attributes the GDPR treats as special-category data, such as ethnic origin or health. GDPR Article 9 bans processing them unless an exception applies. The AI Act supplies one, limited to what is strictly necessary to detect and correct bias.

### As enacted vs as amended
- **As enacted (Art. 10(5)):** providers of high-risk systems only, tied to the Article 10(2)(f)-(g) bias examination.
- **As amended by the Digital Omnibus (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force 27 July 2026):** Article 10(5) is deleted and the rule moves to new **Article 4a**. Paragraph 1 keeps the high-risk provider rule. Paragraph 2 extends it to providers and deployers of other AI systems and models and to deployers of high-risk systems. It creates no duty to run bias testing.

### The six conditions
1. Other data, including synthetic or anonymised data, cannot do the job.
2. Re-use limits, state-of-the-art security and pseudonymisation.
3. Strict, documented access controls and confidentiality duties.
4. No transmission or transfer to other parties.
5. Deletion once the bias is corrected or retention ends, whichever is first.
6. Processing records explain why it was strictly necessary.

The GDPR applies on top.
term:Special-Category Data for Bias Dete.exam_tip: Rule out synthetic or anonymised data first; pseudonymisation is a required safeguard on the sensitive data itself. An Article 10(5) anchor means high-risk providers only, while Article 4a also reaches other systems, models and deployers.

term:Automatic Logging (Art. 12).deep_dive:
### What the system must log
Article 12 is a design requirement: a high-risk system must technically allow automatic recording of events for its whole lifetime. Logging must give traceability suited to the intended purpose and capture events relevant to:

- situations where the system may present a risk (Art. 79(1)) or has undergone a substantial modification;
- the provider's post-market monitoring (Art. 72);
- the deployer's monitoring of operation (Art. 26(5)).

For remote biometric identification (Annex III point 1(a)) the minimum content is fixed: start and end of each use, the reference database checked, the input data that produced a match, and the people who verified the result under Article 14(5).

### Who keeps them, and for how long
Providers keep logs under their control for a period suited to the purpose, at least six months (Art. 19). Deployers have the same floor for logs they control (Art. 26(6)). Other EU or national law, data-protection law in particular, can set a different period. Article 18 is separate: the provider keeps technical documentation, QMS documentation, notified-body decisions and the EU declaration of conformity for 10 years after market placement.
term:Automatic Logging (Art. 12).exam_tip: Six months is the floor for logs, for providers and deployers alike; 10 years is for documentation. A question on why logging exists wants traceability for investigation, audit and post-market monitoring.

term:Two-Person Verification Rule (Art..deep_dive:
### The rule
Article 14 requires every high-risk system to be designed so people can oversee it effectively. Paragraph 5 adds a safeguard for one category: remote biometric identification systems in Annex III point 1(a). The deployer may take no action or decision based on an identification unless at least two natural persons, each with the necessary competence, training and authority, have separately verified and confirmed it.

### The exception
The rule does not apply to systems used for law enforcement, migration, border control or asylum where Union or national law considers it disproportionate. The carve-out depends on that legal determination.

### How it connects
- Article 12(3) makes the identities of the verifying people part of the minimum log content for these systems, so the second check leaves an audit trail.
- One-to-one biometric verification that only confirms a person is who they claim to be is excluded from Annex III point 1(a), so the rule does not reach it.
- Real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces for law enforcement is a separate question, prohibited by Article 5(1)(h) outside three narrow exceptions.

term:Accuracy, Robustness and Cybersecur.deep_dive:
### Three properties, one article
Article 15 requires a high-risk system to reach accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity levels suited to its purpose, and to keep performing consistently on all three for its whole lifecycle.

### Accuracy
The provider declares accuracy levels and the metrics behind them in the instructions for use (Art. 15(3); Art. 13(3)(b)(ii)), so a deployer can judge fit for its context.

### Robustness
The system must be as resilient as possible to errors, faults and inconsistencies, including those caused by people or other systems it interacts with. Technical redundancy, such as backup or fail-safe plans, is the named route. Systems that keep learning after release must limit feedback loops, where biased outputs become future inputs (Art. 15(4)).

### Cybersecurity
The system must resist unauthorised attempts to alter its use, outputs or performance. Article 15(5) names the AI-specific threats to prevent, detect, respond to, resolve and control: data poisoning, poisoning of pre-trained components (model poisoning), adversarial examples or model evasion, confidentiality attacks, and model flaws.

### Presumptions
A Cybersecurity Act certificate or statement of conformity presumes the cybersecurity part is met (Art. 42(2)). As amended by the 2026 Digital Omnibus, systems that meet the Cyber Resilience Act's conditions are deemed compliant too (Art. 42(3)).
term:Accuracy, Robustness and Cybersecur.exam_tip: The testable piece is the Article 15(5) attack list: data and model poisoning (training time), adversarial examples or evasion (inference time), confidentiality attacks, model flaws. Backup and fail-safe plans sit under robustness, not cybersecurity.

term:Presumption of Conformity (Art. 40).deep_dive:
### How the presumption works
EU product law offers a shortcut to proving compliance: follow a European harmonised standard and, once its reference is published in the Official Journal, conformity with the requirements it covers is presumed. Article 40 applies this to the high-risk requirements (Chapter III, Section 2) and to the GPAI obligations in Chapter V. The presumption reaches only as far as the standard's coverage.

### Fallbacks and partial presumptions
- **Common specifications (Art. 41):** where standards are refused, late, non-compliant with the request or weak on fundamental rights, and none is expected soon, the Commission may adopt them by implementing act; following them also gives a presumption.
- **Article 42:** training and test data reflecting the system's actual geographical, behavioural, contextual or functional setting are presumed to meet Article 10(4); a Cybersecurity Act certificate presumes Article 15 cybersecurity.

### What does not count
An ISO/IEC 42001 certificate, NIST AI RMF alignment or an ISO/IEC 42005 impact assessment builds evidence but creates no legal presumption. Adhering to the GPAI Code of Practice helps demonstrate compliance with Articles 53 and 55 without creating one.

### Status
EN 18286:2026, the CEN-CENELEC quality management standard aimed at Article 17, was published in July 2026. It gives a presumption only once its reference is cited in the Official Journal.
term:Presumption of Conformity (Art. 40).exam_tip: Any option claiming that ISO 42001 certification or signing the GPAI Code of Practice gives a presumption of conformity is wrong. The presumption attaches to harmonised standards cited in the Official Journal, or to Commission common specifications.

term:EU Database Registration (Art. 49).deep_dive:
### Who registers what
- **Providers** (or their authorised representative) register themselves and each Annex III high-risk system before placing it on the market or putting it into service (Art. 49(1)). Annex I product systems fall outside this duty.
- **Providers relying on the Article 6(3) derogation**, who conclude that an Annex III system is not high-risk, still register it (Art. 49(2)). As amended by the 2026 Digital Omnibus the entry asks for less: no summary of grounds and no list of Member States.
- **Deployers that are public authorities** or EU bodies register themselves, select the system and register their use (Art. 49(3)). They must not use a high-risk system missing from the database (Art. 26(8)).

### Who sees it
The Commission sets up and maintains the database with the Member States and is its controller (Art. 71). Most entries are public and machine-readable. Entries for law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control uses (Annex III points 1, 6 and 7) go in a secure non-public section open only to the Commission and designated national authorities (Art. 49(4)). Critical infrastructure systems (Annex III point 2) are registered at national level (Art. 49(5)).

### Sequence
Conformity assessment, then the declaration of conformity, then CE marking, then registration.
