term:Transparency Obligations (Art. 50).deep_dive:
### Four paragraphs, two actors
- **50(1) Provider, interaction:** systems meant to interact directly with people must be designed so people know they are dealing with AI, unless that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person.
- **50(2) Provider, marking:** systems generating synthetic audio, image, video or text must mark output in a machine-readable, detectable way, so far as technically feasible. Assistive editing that does not substantially alter the input is exempt.
- **50(3) Deployer, emotion recognition and biometric categorisation:** inform the people exposed that the system is operating, and process their data under the GDPR.
- **50(4) Deployer, deepfakes and text:** disclose that image, audio or video deepfakes are artificial; for evidently artistic, satirical or fictional work, disclose in a way that does not spoil it. Disclose AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, unless a human reviewed it and someone holds editorial responsibility.

### Timing and form
Clear, distinguishable, accessible, and no later than the first interaction or exposure (50(5)). Uses authorised by law to fight crime are largely exempt.

### Dates
From 2 August 2026. As amended by the 2026 Digital Omnibus, generative systems already on the market before then have until 2 December 2026 to add marking (Art. 111(4)).
term:Transparency Obligations (Art. 50).exam_tip: Split by actor: chatbot disclosure and machine-readable marking are provider duties; emotion-recognition notices, deepfake labels and public-interest text disclosure are deployer duties. A satirical deepfake still needs disclosure, made in a way that does not spoil the work, and a notice shown only when the user leaves is too late.

term:AI Act Milestone: 2 Aug 2026.deep_dive:
2 August 2026 is the Act's general date of application under Article 113, and its meaning changed with the Digital Omnibus.

As enacted (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), this was the date the Annex III high-risk rules took effect, including conformity assessment and CE marking, and the date the Article 50 transparency duties began. Full application across all provisions was expected by 2027.

As amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the high-risk block moved out. What still applies from 2 August 2026 is Article 50 transparency (chatbot disclosure, machine-readable marking of synthetic content, deepfake and public-interest text labelling) and the Commission's GPAI enforcement powers, including Article 101 fines of up to 3% or EUR 15 million. The national regulatory sandbox deadline also moved off this date, to 2 August 2027.

So on this single date the two legal states agree only in part. An item saying high-risk rules apply from 2 August 2026 is anchored in the original text. An item saying transparency and GPAI enforcement is correct under both.

One related sub-date: generative systems already on the market before 2 August 2026 have until 2 December 2026 to add Article 50(2) machine-readable marking, under the new Article 111(4).
term:AI Act Milestone: 2 Aug 2026.exam_tip: Under both texts this date brings Article 50 transparency and the Commission's GPAI enforcement powers, including Article 101 fines. As enacted it also started Annex III high-risk duties; the Omnibus moved those to 2 December 2027. A stem saying high-risk rules apply from this date is anchored in the original text.

term:AI Act Milestone: 2 Aug 2028.deep_dive:
This is the amended date for high-risk requirements on product-embedded AI: systems that are, or are safety components of, a product covered by the Annex I harmonisation legislation, which is the Article 6(1) route to high-risk. Medical devices, machinery and vehicles are the examples to hold.

As enacted, this milestone was 2 August 2027. The Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, moved it to 2 August 2028 by replacing Article 113(c)(ii). The rationale is structural: Annex I systems already sit inside a sectoral conformity regime, so the AI Act requirements flow through that sectoral legislation, and alignment takes longer.

The Annex I route and the Annex III route are the two independent ways a system becomes high-risk, and they run on different clocks. Annex III, the use-case route covering recruitment or credit scoring, applies from 2 December 2027 as amended. Annex I, the product-safety route covering safety components, applies from 2 August 2028 as amended.

The Omnibus also moved the machinery sector. Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 shifted to Annex I Section B, so AI requirements reach it through sectoral delegated acts rather than the full high-risk regime, and non-safety functions such as user assistance or convenience are not safety components (Article 6(1a) to (1c)).
term:AI Act Milestone: 2 Aug 2028.exam_tip: Annex I and Article 6(1) product-embedded high-risk: 2 August 2027 as enacted, 2 August 2028 as amended. Annex III is 2 December 2027 as amended. Do not confuse the as-enacted 2 August 2027 with the GPAI legacy-model deadline, which falls on the same day.

term:AI Act Milestone: 2 Dec 2027.deep_dive:
This is the amended date for the biggest block of AI Act obligations: the high-risk requirements for Annex III systems. Chapter III, Sections 1 to 3, carry Articles 8 to 15 (the requirements), Articles 16 to 27 (operator duties) and the conformity, CE marking and registration machinery. For an Annex III system this date is when that whole chain begins to apply, including the Article 26 deployer duties and the Article 27 fundamental rights impact assessment for public bodies, private entities providing public services, and credit and insurance use cases.

As enacted, this milestone was 2 August 2026. The Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, moved it to 2 December 2027 by replacing Article 113(c)(i).

Annex III is the use-case route to high-risk: biometrics; critical infrastructure; education and vocational training; employment and worker management; access to essential private and public services including credit scoring; law enforcement; migration, asylum and border control; and the administration of justice and democratic processes. A system in one of those areas is high-risk unless the Article 6(3) derogation applies, and a system that performs profiling is always high-risk.

Do not confuse this with the Annex I date (2 August 2028), or with Article 111(2), which catches a legacy high-risk system already on the market before its category date only if the design changes significantly afterward.

Annex I sits later, at 2 August 2028 as amended. Do not confuse with 2 December 2026, when the two new Article 5 bans start.

term:AI Act Milestone: 2 Feb 2025.deep_dive:
2 February 2025 is the first substantive milestone. Two chapters began to apply: Chapter I definitions, and the Chapter II obligations, which are the Article 5 prohibitions and the Article 4 AI literacy duty.

The prohibitions. As enacted, Article 5(1) lists eight practices: subliminal or purposefully manipulative techniques that distort behaviour; exploitation of vulnerabilities tied to age, disability or social or economic situation; social scoring by public or private actors; individual criminal-offence risk prediction based solely on profiling; untargeted scraping of facial images to build recognition databases; emotion recognition in workplaces and educational institutions; biometric categorisation by sensitive traits; and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces, with narrow law-enforcement exceptions requiring prior judicial or independent authorisation.

AI literacy. Article 4 required providers and deployers to take measures to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among their staff. As amended by the 2026 Digital Omnibus, the duty became one of taking measures to support literacy, with no guaranteed level for any individual, and the softened wording applies from 27 July 2026.

This date did not move. The eight prohibitions have applied since 2 February 2025 in both legal states. Only the two Omnibus additions, intimate imagery and CSAM, start later, on 2 December 2026, and they bring the list to ten.
term:AI Act Milestone: 2 Feb 2025.exam_tip: This date means prohibitions plus AI literacy, the first obligations to apply. Eight prohibited practices as enacted, ten as amended (the two new ones from 2 December 2026). The Omnibus did not move this date.

term:GPAI Code of Practice (Art. 56).deep_dive:
Article 56 is the legal basis for codes of practice in the AI Act. It directs the AI Office to encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes covering the GPAI obligations in Articles 53 and 55, to be ready by 2 May 2025; if they were not finalised by 2 August 2025, the Commission could set common rules by implementing act. The GPAI Code of Practice was published on 10 July 2025, and the Commission and the AI Board confirmed its adequacy on 1 August 2025.

What adherence buys is the exam point, and it is narrow. A provider that adheres to a code assessed as adequate has a straightforward way to demonstrate compliance with Articles 53 and 55. It is not conclusive evidence of compliance, not a safe harbor, and not a presumption of conformity. Under Articles 53(4) and 55(2), only a harmonised standard, once its reference is published in the Official Journal, gives a presumption of conformity. A non-adherent must show "alternative adequate means", for example a gap analysis against the code. Keeping code commitments can count as a mitigating factor when a fine is set (Article 101(1)).

As amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, Article 56(6) has the Commission, taking utmost account of the Board's opinion, assess whether codes cover Articles 53 and 55 and publish that assessment. The replaced paragraph no longer contains the old sentence letting the Commission give a code "general validity" by implementing act.
term:GPAI Code of Practice (Art. 56).exam_tip: Article 56 is the codes-of-practice basis and the GPAI Code is voluntary. Adherence demonstrates compliance and can count as a mitigating factor for fines, but it is not a safe harbor and not a presumption of conformity; only harmonised standards give that (Articles 53(4), 55(2)). Do not confuse it with the Article 50(7) marking and labelling code.

term:Scope and Extraterritorial Reach (A.deep_dive:
The Act follows the EU market and EU use of AI output. Where a company is headquartered does not decide whether it is caught.

### Who is in scope (Art. 2(1))
- Providers placing AI systems or general-purpose AI models on the EU market, or putting systems into service there, wherever they are established.
- Deployers established or located in the EU.
- Providers and deployers in third countries where the system's output is used in the EU. Recital 22 gives the reason: otherwise an EU firm could send EU data to a contractor abroad, have a high-risk system process it there, and import only the result.
- Importers and distributors.
- Product manufacturers that ship an AI system with their product under their own name.
- Authorised representatives of non-EU providers.
- Affected persons located in the EU.

Art. 3(8) groups six of these roles (provider, product manufacturer, deployer, authorised representative, importer, distributor) as 'operators'.

### Worked example
A US vendor with no EU office sells a CV-screening tool to German employers. The vendor is the provider of a high-risk system and must appoint an EU authorised representative (Art. 22); each employer is a deployer. The AI Act's territorial test is separate from GDPR Art. 3, so one law can apply where the other does not.
term:Scope and Extraterritorial Reach (A.exam_tip: Establishment is never the test. A non-EU firm that sells into the EU, or whose system's output is used in the EU, is caught, and a non-EU provider of a high-risk system or GPAI model must appoint an EU authorised representative.

term:Scope Exclusions (Art. 2).deep_dive:
### The carve-outs
- **Military, defence, national security (Art. 2(3)):** excluded only where use is exclusively for those purposes, whatever kind of entity runs it. Recital 24 adds that a system marketed for both military and civilian or law-enforcement purposes is in scope, and a military system later used for civilian purposes comes into scope for whoever uses it that way.
- **Third-country public authorities (Art. 2(4)):** excluded when using AI under international law-enforcement or judicial cooperation agreements with adequate fundamental-rights safeguards.
- **Scientific R&D (Art. 2(6)):** systems and models specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research.
- **Pre-market R&D (Art. 2(8)):** research, testing and development before placing on the market or putting into service. Testing in real-world conditions is not covered.
- **Personal use (Art. 2(10)):** individuals using AI for purely personal, non-professional activity owe no deployer duties.
- **Open source (Art. 2(12)):** systems under free and open-source licences, unless placed on the market or put into service as high-risk systems or as systems falling under Art. 5 or Art. 50.

### Do not confuse
General-purpose AI models follow a different open-source rule. Art. 53(2) waives only the Art. 53(1)(a)-(b) documentation duties, and Art. 54(6) the authorised representative, never for systemic-risk models. The copyright policy and training-content summary always apply.
term:Scope Exclusions (Art. 2).exam_tip: Watch the word 'exclusively': a dual-use military and civilian system is in scope. Open source does not rescue a high-risk system, a prohibited practice or an Art. 50 transparency case, and national security is outside the Act rather than an Art. 5 exception.

term:AI Literacy (Art. 4).deep_dive:
### What the duty covers
Art. 3(56) defines AI literacy as the skills, knowledge and understanding that let providers, deployers and affected persons deploy AI in an informed way and recognise its opportunities, risks and possible harms. Art. 4 makes providers and deployers act on it for their staff and for others operating or using AI systems on their behalf, such as contractors. Measures should reflect those people's technical knowledge, experience, education and training, the context of use, and the people the system will be used on.

It applies whatever the risk tier, and it started alongside the prohibitions on 2 February 2025.

### The 2026 change
The Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) replaced Art. 4 from 27 July 2026. Providers and deployers must now take measures to support the development of AI literacy, and the text says they need not guarantee any specific level for any individual. New paragraphs require the Commission and Member States to support compliance, especially for SMEs, have the Commission publish practical examples, and have the AI Board adopt recommendations.

### In practice
Role-based training fits the text: executives, developers and frontline operators need different content. The Article demands no certificate, and the fixed fine tiers in Art. 99 do not list Art. 4.
term:AI Literacy (Art. 4).exam_tip: Art. 4 binds providers and deployers of all AI systems, not only high-risk ones, and has applied since 2 February 2025. If the stem anchors to the 2026 Omnibus, the answer is 'take measures to support', with no guaranteed level for any individual.

term:Placing on the Market vs. Putting i.deep_dive:
Three Art. 3 definitions decide when obligations attach and who carries them.

- **Placing on the market (Art. 3(9)):** the first making available of an AI system or general-purpose AI model on the Union market.
- **Making available on the market (Art. 3(10)):** any supply for distribution or use on the Union market in the course of a commercial activity, paid or free. Distributors make systems available; they do not place them.
- **Putting into service (Art. 3(11)):** supplying a system for first use directly to a deployer, or for the supplier's own use, in the EU for its intended purpose.

### Why it matters
A provider is whoever develops a system or general-purpose AI model, or has one developed, and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name or trademark, paid or free (Art. 3(3)). A bank that builds a credit-scoring model for its own lending sells nothing, yet it puts the system into service. It is the provider of a high-risk system and also its deployer.

Provider duties such as conformity assessment and registration must be met before either event. Pre-market research, testing and development sit outside the Act until one of them happens (Art. 2(8)), but testing in real-world conditions does not.
term:Placing on the Market vs. Putting i.exam_tip: Building AI for in-house use does not avoid provider duties, because putting into service for own use counts. 'Placing on the market' is the first supply only; distributors later 'make available'.

term:Right to Explanation (Art. 86).deep_dive:
### The right
Article 86 gives an affected person a right against the deployer, not the provider. It applies when the deployer takes a decision on the basis of output from an Annex III high-risk system (point 2, critical infrastructure, excluded) and the decision produces legal effects, or similarly significantly affects the person in a way they consider harmful to their health, safety or fundamental rights. The person can obtain clear and meaningful explanations of:
- the role the AI system played in the decision-making procedure; and
- the main elements of the decision taken.

### Limits
- Exceptions or restrictions in EU law, or national law consistent with it, take priority.
- The right applies only to the extent other Union law does not already provide it, so where GDPR Article 22 and Article 15(1)(h) already give meaningful information about the logic of a solely automated decision, those rules apply first.

### How it differs from the GDPR
GDPR Article 22 needs a decision based solely on automated processing. Article 86 has no such condition, so it reaches decisions a human took on the basis of the system's output.

A separate remedy: anyone may complain to a market surveillance authority about an infringement of the Act (Art. 85).
term:Right to Explanation (Art. 86).exam_tip: Article 86 points at the deployer and asks for the role of the AI system plus the main elements of the decision. Replying that the model is proprietary, or referring the person to the vendor, does not discharge the deployer's duty.

term:AI Regulatory Sandbox (Art. 57).deep_dive:
### What it is
A controlled environment set up by a competent authority in which a provider or prospective provider develops, trains, tests and validates an innovative AI system for a limited time before market placement, following a sandbox plan agreed with the authority. It may include supervised testing in real-world conditions.

### Deadlines
Each Member State must have at least one national sandbox operational, alone or jointly with others: by 2 August 2026 as enacted, 2 August 2027 as amended by the 2026 Digital Omnibus. The amendment also lets the AI Office run a Union-level sandbox for systems under its own competence, with priority access for SMEs, start-ups and small mid-caps.

### What participants get
- guidance on regulatory expectations and supervision of risks to fundamental rights, health and safety;
- written proof of activities and an exit report, which notified bodies and market surveillance authorities take into account to speed up conformity assessment;
- no administrative fines under the Act if they follow the plan and act in good faith on the authority's guidance.

### What they keep
Participants remain liable under EU and national liability law for damage to third parties during the experiment, and the authority can suspend testing where significant risks cannot be mitigated.
term:AI Regulatory Sandbox (Art. 57).exam_tip: A sandbox buys supervised testing time and protection from AI Act fines for good-faith participants; civil liability and the authority's power to suspend remain. Date anchor: national sandboxes due 2 August 2026 as enacted, 2 August 2027 after the Omnibus.

term:GPAI Model vs. GPAI System.deep_dive:
### Two objects, two rulebooks
The AI Act regulates the model and the system separately. A general-purpose AI model (Art. 3(63)) is the trained artifact: it shows significant generality, performs a wide range of distinct tasks competently and can be integrated into many downstream systems. Recital 97 says a model is not an AI system on its own; it needs further components, such as a user interface. Its provider owes Arts. 53 to 55.

A general-purpose AI system (Art. 3(66)) is an AI system based on a GPAI model that can serve many purposes, used directly or built into other systems. It is regulated like any AI system, by what it does:
- Art. 50(2) marking of synthetic content falls on providers of AI systems, including GPAI systems.
- A party that changes a GPAI system's intended purpose so it becomes high-risk is treated as its provider (Art. 25(1)(c)).

### Where the roles meet
A company that integrates a model into its own system, whether the model is its own or licensed, is a downstream provider (Art. 3(68)) and the provider of that system. Where one provider builds both, model duties and system duties apply together (recital 97). Under amended Art. 75(1)(a) the AI Office supervises such systems, with carve-outs such as Annex I products.
term:GPAI Model vs. GPAI System.exam_tip: First decide whether the stem is about the model (Arts. 53-55, owed by whoever trained it) or the system (Art. 50, high-risk rules, owed by whoever built the product). A company that builds a product on another firm's model is the provider of that system; the model duties stay with the model provider.

term:GPAI Model with Systemic Risk (Art..deep_dive:
### What systemic risk means
Art. 3(65) ties systemic risk to high-impact capabilities, meaning capabilities that match or exceed those of the most advanced models (Art. 3(64)). The risk must have a significant impact on the EU market, through reach or through foreseeable harm to public health, safety, public security, fundamental rights or society, and be able to spread at scale along the value chain.

### Two ways in
- **Capability route (Art. 51(1)(a)).** High-impact capabilities judged with technical tools, indicators and benchmarks. Art. 51(2) presumes them once cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOP. The provider can contest that in its Art. 52 notification.
- **Designation route (Art. 51(1)(b)).** The Commission decides, on its own initiative or after a qualified alert from the Scientific Panel of independent experts (Art. 90), that a model has equivalent capabilities or impact. It weighs the Annex XIII criteria: parameters, data set size, training compute, modalities, benchmarks, autonomy and tool access, number of registered end users, and reach, which is presumed once at least 10,000 registered EU business users have access.

The Commission can change the thresholds by delegated act (Art. 51(3)) and publishes the list of systemic-risk models (Art. 52(6)). Classification adds Art. 55 (evaluations, systemic-risk mitigation, serious-incident reporting, cybersecurity) on top of Arts. 53 and 54, and ends any open-source relief.
term:GPAI Model with Systemic Risk (Art..exam_tip: Only training compute above 10^25 FLOP triggers the presumption; user counts, open-source status and modality never do. A model below that line can still be designated by the Commission under Annex XIII, often after a Scientific Panel alert.

term:Systemic-Risk Notification (Art. 52.deep_dive:
### The two-week clock
Art. 52(1) requires a provider whose model meets the Art. 51(1)(a) condition to notify the Commission without delay, and in any event within two weeks of meeting it or of learning that it will. Large training runs are planned with compute allocated up front, so recital 112 and the Commission's GPAI guidelines expect providers to estimate compute before the main run and to notify before training ends where crossing 10^25 FLOP is reasonably foreseeable. The notification gives the compute estimate in FLOP to two significant figures and the method behind it.

### Contesting the classification
- With the notification, the provider may submit substantiated arguments that, exceptionally, the model does not present systemic risk (Art. 52(2)). The guidelines put the burden of proof on the provider, usually met with benchmark results showing no high-impact capabilities.
- If the Commission finds the arguments insufficient, it rejects them and the model counts as systemic-risk (Art. 52(3)).
- If the Commission learns of an unnotified systemic-risk model, it can designate it (Art. 52(1), (4)).
- A designated model can be reassessed on a reasoned request with new reasons, no earlier than six months after the decision (Art. 52(5)).

The Commission publishes and updates the list of systemic-risk models (Art. 52(6)).
term:Systemic-Risk Notification (Art. 52.exam_tip: When a training run will cross 10^25 FLOP, the correct action is to notify the Commission within two weeks; halting training or waiting to be designated are distractors. Any argument that the model is not systemic goes in with the notification, and the Commission decides.

term:Public Summary of Training Content.deep_dive:
### The duty
Art. 53(1)(d) requires every GPAI provider to draw up and publish a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used to train its model, using the AI Office template. Its purpose is to help rightsholders enforce their rights (recital 107), so it should be generally comprehensive in scope rather than technically detailed, for example naming the main data collections and describing other sources in narrative form, while trade secrets stay protected.

### The template (24 July 2025)
Three sections:
- **General information:** provider, model, modalities and training data size in broad ranges.
- **List of data sources:** public data sets, licensed private data sets, crawled and scraped web content, user data, synthetic data and other sources. For scraped content, the top 10% of domain names by content size; SMEs list the top 5% or 1,000 domains, whichever is lower.
- **Relevant data processing:** how rights reservations were respected and illegal content removed.

### Timing and limits
Publish no later than market placement. If the provider trains the model further on new data, it updates the summary every six months, or sooner if the new data materially changes it. The AI Office does not check work by work. Open-source release does not exempt the duty (recital 104). Models placed before 2 August 2025 publish by 2 August 2027 and explain any gaps.
term:Public Summary of Training Content.exam_tip: Choose the answer that describes a summary on the AI Office template, comprehensive in scope but never a list of every work or data set. Open-source providers still owe it, and it is a separate duty from the Art. 53(1)(c) copyright policy.

term:Open-Source GPAI Exemption (Art. 53.deep_dive:
### What it lifts
Art. 53(2) and Art. 54(6) exempt a qualifying open-source GPAI provider from three duties only:
- Annex XI technical documentation for the AI Office (Art. 53(1)(a));
- Annex XII information for downstream providers (Art. 53(1)(b));
- appointing an EU authorised representative (Art. 54).

### What it never lifts
The copyright policy (Art. 53(1)(c)) and the public training-content summary (Art. 53(1)(d)) still apply, because publishing weights reveals little about training data or copyright compliance (recital 104). A systemic-risk model gets no relief at all.

### Conditions in the Commission's GPAI guidelines
- The licence must let anyone access, use, modify and redistribute the model. Non-commercial or research-only terms, bans on redistribution, user-scale thresholds and separate commercial licences disqualify it. Proportionate, safety-oriented use restrictions are allowed.
- No monetisation (recital 103). Dual licensing with paid commercial use, paid services without which the model cannot be used, and hosting only on a platform that charges or serves paid ads all count. Requiring users' personal data for access counts too, unless the processing serves only model security.
- Weights, architecture and usage information must be public.

Art. 2(12) is a different carve-out: it takes open-source AI systems out of the Act unless they are high-risk, prohibited or caught by Art. 50.
term:Open-Source GPAI Exemption (Art. 53.exam_tip: Open weights remove only the technical documentation, the downstream information pack and the EU representative. The copyright policy and training summary survive, and a systemic-risk model gets no relief.

term:Downstream Modifier (GPAI).deep_dive:
### The test
The Commission's guidelines treat a downstream modifier as provider of the modified GPAI model only where the change is significant in generality, capabilities or systemic risk. The indicative criterion: compute used for the modification exceeds one third of the compute used to train the original. If the modifier cannot know or estimate that figure, it uses one third of 10^25 FLOP when the original is a systemic-risk model, and one third of 10^23 FLOP otherwise.

### Consequences once over the line
- Duties are limited to the modification (recital 109): document the changes and new training data, keep a copyright policy and publish a training-content summary covering the modification data, and appoint an EU representative if established outside the EU.
- Modifying a systemic-risk model past the threshold makes the result a systemic-risk model, so the modifier notifies the Commission under Art. 52 and meets Art. 55.

### Keep it apart from system roles
This rule decides who provides the **model**. A company that builds a product on a model, modified or not, is still the provider of that **AI system**. Under Art. 25(1), putting its name on a high-risk system, substantially modifying one, or changing a system's purpose to high-risk makes it the high-risk provider, whatever compute it used.
term:Downstream Modifier (GPAI).exam_tip: A fine-tune using about 10% of the original compute does not make the company the model's provider; the indicative line is more than one third. Do not confuse it with the 10^23 FLOP criterion for whether a model counts as GPAI at all.

term:Commission GPAI Enforcement Powers.deep_dive:
### Who enforces, and from when
Art. 88 gives the Commission exclusive power to supervise and enforce the GPAI chapter and entrusts the work to the AI Office. National market surveillance authorities can ask the Commission to act but cannot enforce Chapter V themselves. The obligations have applied since 2 August 2025; the enforcement powers, fines included, since 2 August 2026.

### The toolkit
- **Monitoring and complaints (Art. 89):** the AI Office tracks compliance, including adherence to codes of practice. Downstream providers can lodge reasoned complaints against a GPAI provider.
- **Information requests (Art. 91):** the Art. 53 and 55 documentation plus anything else needed to assess compliance.
- **Evaluations (Art. 92):** after consulting the AI Board, the AI Office can evaluate a model through APIs or source-code access, directly or through independent experts.
- **Measures (Art. 93):** comply with Arts. 53-54, apply mitigations after an evaluation finds a serious systemic-risk concern, or restrict, withdraw or recall the model. A systemic-risk provider can offer commitments that the Commission makes binding.
- **Fines (Art. 101):** up to €15M or 3% of worldwide turnover, whichever is higher, for intentional or negligent breaches, ignored requests or measures, misleading information or refused model access. Code commitments count when the fine is set, and the CJEU has unlimited review.
term:Commission GPAI Enforcement Powers.exam_tip: GPAI enforcement belongs to the Commission through the AI Office, never to national authorities, and it began on 2 August 2026, a year after the obligations. The GPAI fine ceiling is 3% or €15M, below the 7% prohibited-practice tier.

term:EU AI Act Governance Bodies.deep_dive:
### EU level
- **AI Office:** part of the Commission. Exclusive GPAI enforcer; as amended in 2026, also supervises some AI systems.
- **European AI Board (Arts. 65-66):** one representative per Member State, three-year term renewable once. The EDPS observes; the AI Office attends without a vote and runs the secretariat. It coordinates national authorities and advises; it has no enforcement power.
- **Advisory Forum (Art. 67):** industry, SMEs, civil society and academia, appointed by the Commission. The Fundamental Rights Agency, ENISA, CEN, CENELEC and ETSI are permanent members.
- **Scientific Panel (Arts. 68, 90):** independent experts, free of ties to any provider. It can send the AI Office a qualified alert that a GPAI model poses Union-level risk or meets Art. 51, which can lead to designation. It orders nothing itself. Sixty experts were appointed on 1 June 2026, as was the Forum.

### National level
Each Member State names at least one **notifying authority**, which designates and monitors notified bodies, and at least one **market surveillance authority**, which polices AI on the market and receives complaints (Art. 70). One market surveillance authority is the single point of contact.

### EU institutions
When an EU institution uses AI, the **EDPS** supervises it and can fine it up to €1.5M for prohibited practices and €750,000 otherwise (Art. 100).
term:EU AI Act Governance Bodies.exam_tip: Match the verb to the body: the AI Office enforces GPAI rules, the Board coordinates, the Advisory Forum gives stakeholder input, the Scientific Panel alerts, national market surveillance authorities police systems and take complaints, notifying authorities oversee notified bodies, and the EDPS supervises EU institutions.

term:Notified Body.deep_dive:
### Who it is
A notified body is a conformity assessment body, an organisation that does third-party testing, certification and inspection, that a Member State has formally notified under the AI Act. It must have legal personality under national law, be independent of the provider and its competitors, carry liability insurance and employ staff who understand the AI systems it assesses (Art. 31).

### Three national actors, three jobs
- **Notifying authority (Art. 28):** assesses, designates and monitors conformity assessment bodies, and can hand the assessment work to the national accreditation body. It notifies the Commission and other Member States, listing the AI system types each body covers (Art. 30, using Annex XIV codes added in 2026).
- **Notified body:** certifies a system before it reaches the market.
- **Market surveillance authority:** polices systems after they reach the market.

### When you need one
Most Annex III high-risk systems (points 2 to 8) use internal control under Annex VI, with no notified body. Annex III point 1 biometric systems need the Annex VII route with a notified body unless the provider fully applies harmonised standards or common specifications. Annex I products follow their sectoral procedure. Certificates last at most four years for Annex III and five for Annex I, can be renewed after reassessment, and can be suspended or withdrawn (Art. 44).
term:Notified Body.exam_tip: Notified bodies certify before market entry, market surveillance authorities enforce after it, and notifying authorities appoint and monitor notified bodies. For most Annex III systems the provider self-assesses, so a notified body is the exception.

term:Right to Lodge a Complaint (Art. 85.deep_dive:
### Who can complain, and to whom
Art. 85 lets any natural or legal person with grounds to believe the Act has been breached submit a complaint to the relevant market surveillance authority. Competitors and civil society groups can use it too, not only affected people. A complaint usually goes to a national body. The exception is a system the AI Office supervises with market surveillance powers, such as one built on the same provider's own GPAI model (Art. 75(1), widened in 2026).

### What a complaint does
The authority uses complaints when planning and conducting market surveillance under Regulation (EU) 2019/1020, following its own procedures. A complaint prompts regulatory action and pays no compensation; damages come through national civil liability law or the Product Liability Directive. Art. 85 sits alongside other administrative and judicial remedies.

### Related channels
- **Art. 89(2):** a downstream provider can send the AI Office a reasoned complaint about the provider of the GPAI model it integrates.
- **Art. 86:** a person affected by a deployer's decision based on an Annex III high-risk system (critical infrastructure excluded) can ask the deployer for an explanation.
- **Art. 87:** whistleblowers reporting infringements are protected under Directive (EU) 2019/1937.
- GDPR complaints about the same system still go to a data protection authority; the AI Act has no lead-authority mechanism.
term:Right to Lodge a Complaint (Art. 85.exam_tip: An individual's AI Act complaint goes to the market surveillance authority, normally the national one, not the EDPB or a GDPR lead authority. The AI Office receives complaints from downstream providers about GPAI model providers (Art. 89(2)) and handles systems it supervises directly.

term:AI Act Milestone: 2 Aug 2025.deep_dive:
### What started
Under Art. 113(b), four blocks of the Act began to apply on 2 August 2025:
- **Chapter V:** the GPAI duties in Arts. 51 to 56, including systemic-risk notification and the Art. 53 documentation, copyright and training-summary duties. The Commission could take Art. 52 classification decisions from this date.
- **Chapter VII:** governance, so the AI Office, AI Board, Advisory Forum, Scientific Panel and national competent authorities had to be in place.
- **Chapter III Section 4:** notifying authorities and notified bodies, so third-party assessment capacity exists before the high-risk rules arrive.
- **Chapter XII and Art. 78:** the penalty framework and confidentiality rules.

Member States had to designate their notifying and market surveillance authorities and adopt national penalty rules by this date.

### The carve-out
Art. 101, the Commission's power to fine GPAI providers, was excluded. GPAI duties therefore applied for a year before they could be fined; enforcement powers started on 2 August 2026. Models already on the market before 2 August 2025 have until 2 August 2027 (Art. 111(3)).

### Context
The GPAI Code of Practice was published on 10 July 2025 and confirmed adequate on 1 August 2025, the day before the duties began. The 2026 Digital Omnibus changed none of these dates.
term:AI Act Milestone: 2 Aug 2025.exam_tip: 2 August 2025 means GPAI duties, governance bodies, notified bodies and the penalty chapter, but not GPAI fines, which waited until 2 August 2026. High-risk rules do not start on this date under either version of the Act.

term:AI Act Milestone: 2 Dec 2026.deep_dive:
### Two things start
- **New prohibitions.** The 2026 Digital Omnibus added points (ba) and (bb) to Art. 5(1): AI that generates or manipulates realistic intimate or sexually explicit imagery of an identifiable person without explicit consent, and AI that generates child sexual abuse material. Placing such a system on the market is caught only where that output is its intended purpose, or a reasonably foreseeable, reproducible outcome it lacks reasonable safeguards against. Breaches fall in the top fine tier, €35M or 7%.
- **Legacy marking deadline.** Art. 50(2) requires providers of generative systems, including GPAI systems, to mark outputs in a machine-readable, detectable way from 2 August 2026. New Art. 111(4) gives systems already on the market before that date until 2 December 2026.

### Exam reading
The date does not exist in the Act as enacted, so it only appears in questions anchored to the amended text. The count of prohibited practices changes here: eight as enacted, ten as amended, with the original eight in force since 2 February 2025.

### Do not confuse
2 December 2026 is a year before 2 December 2027, the amended start date for Annex III high-risk rules. New generative systems placed from 2 August 2026 get no grace period; only legacy systems use the December deadline.
term:AI Act Milestone: 2 Dec 2026.exam_tip: 2 December 2026 belongs only to the amended Act: the two new bans plus the marking deadline for generative systems already on the market. Keep it apart from 2 December 2027, the amended Annex III high-risk date.

term:AI Act Milestone: 2 Aug 2027.deep_dive:
### As enacted (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)
Two things land on 2 August 2027:
- **Annex I high-risk rules.** AI that is a safety component of, or is itself, a product under Annex I harmonisation law and needs third-party conformity assessment (Art. 6(1)), such as AI in medical devices or machinery, falls under the high-risk requirements a year after the Annex III systems.
- **GPAI legacy deadline.** Models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 must comply with the GPAI duties (Art. 111(3)).

### As amended (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744)
- Annex I high-risk rules move to **2 August 2028**.
- The GPAI legacy deadline stays at 2 August 2027.
- The national sandbox deadline moves here from 2 August 2026: each Member State must have at least one AI regulatory sandbox operational (Art. 57(1)).

### Related cut-off
AI components of the large-scale EU IT systems in Annex X that are placed on the market before 2 August 2027 have until 31 December 2030 to comply (Art. 111(1)).

### Exam reading
An item saying Annex I rules apply from 2 August 2027 is anchored in the original text. An item about legacy GPAI models gives the same answer under both versions.

term:Alternative Adequate Means (Arts. 5.deep_dive:
### Three ways to show compliance
Arts. 53(4) and 55(2) give a GPAI provider three options:
- comply with a harmonised standard, the only route that gives a presumption of conformity;
- adhere to a code of practice assessed as adequate, such as the GPAI Code, which demonstrates compliance without presuming it;
- show alternative adequate means, assessed by the Commission.

### What the third route costs
Under the Commission's GPAI guidelines, a provider outside an adequate code must report its measures to the AI Office and explain how they meet each duty, for example through a gap analysis against the Code. It can expect more information requests and more requests for model access across the lifecycle, because the AI Office knows less about how it complies. It also loses a benefit at the fining stage: commitments kept under an adequate code can count in mitigation (Art. 101(1)).

### Who uses it
Meta does not appear on the Commission's signatory list of 31 July 2026, so it must show alternative adequate means for every duty. xAI signed only the Safety & Security chapter, so it uses alternative means for the Transparency and Copyright duties. Opting out of one chapter loses the benefit for that chapter only. The legal duties are identical for every provider.
term:Alternative Adequate Means (Arts. 5.exam_tip: Non-signatories owe the same Art. 53 and 55 duties as signatories and differ only in how they prove compliance. Neither the Code nor alternative means gives a presumption of conformity, which only harmonised standards provide.

term:Lawful Basis (GDPR Art. 6).deep_dive:
### The six bases
Art. 6(1) lists them: (a) consent, (b) contract with the person, (c) legal obligation, (d) vital interests, (e) public task, (f) legitimate interests. Every processing operation needs at least one, chosen before processing starts and named in the Art. 13 or 14 notice. None ranks above another (Opinion 28/2024, para 60), so consent is not the default. Public authorities cannot rely on (f) for processing in performance of their tasks.

### Which one fits AI training
- **Consent:** hard to collect at scale and to honour on withdrawal. Draft EDPB Guidelines 03/2026 call it most probably unworkable for large-scale web scraping.
- **Contract:** read narrowly. In *Meta Platforms v Bundeskartellamt* (C-252/21, 4 July 2023) the CJEU held that processing must be objectively indispensable to a purpose integral to the contract; useful is not enough. Training a general model rarely qualifies.
- **Legitimate interests:** the usual route. Opinion 28/2024 applies three cumulative steps: a lawful, real and present interest; necessity (no less intrusive means, proportionate data); and balancing against the person's rights and reasonable expectations. Record it in a legitimate interests assessment (LIA) and expect Art. 21 objections.

### Layers on top
Special-category data also needs an Art. 9(2) exception. Reusing data collected for another purpose runs the Art. 6(4) compatibility test.
term:Lawful Basis (GDPR Art. 6).exam_tip: With no hierarchy among the six, 'get consent' is usually the wrong answer for AI training; legitimate interests with the three-step test and a documented LIA is the expected route. Sensitive data needs two locks: an Art. 6 basis and an Art. 9(2) exception.

term:Right to Object (GDPR Art. 21).deep_dive:
### How Art. 21 works
- **21(1):** a person objects, on grounds relating to their particular situation, to processing based on Art. 6(1)(e) (public task) or (f) (legitimate interests), including profiling. The controller must then stop unless it demonstrates compelling legitimate grounds that override the person's interests, rights and freedoms, or needs the data to establish, exercise or defend legal claims. The burden sits with the controller.
- **21(2)-(3):** an objection to direct marketing, including related profiling, ends that processing with no balancing.
- **21(4):** the controller must bring the right to the person's attention explicitly, at the latest at the first communication, and present it separately from other information.
- **21(5)-(6):** objection by automated means online; a qualified version for research and statistics.

### The AI angle
Developers usually train on legitimate interest, so Art. 21 is the data subject right most likely to reach a training pipeline. EDPB Opinion 28/2024 tells supervisory authorities to check whether the controller can show overriding grounds and whether people can actually exercise the right. It also lists an unconditional opt-out, offered before processing starts and going beyond Art. 21, as a measure that can help a close balancing test. If the model fails the Opinion's anonymity test, objection, access and erasure rights reach the model itself as well as the source records.
term:Right to Object (GDPR Art. 21).exam_tip: Two trap answers recur: 'absolute right', which is true only for direct marketing, and 'refer the objection to the supervisory authority', which the GDPR never requires. For legitimate-interest processing the controller stops unless it can demonstrate compelling legitimate grounds, and that burden is the controller's.

term:Model Weights as Copies (Getty vs..deep_dive:
### The question
Training copies works into a corpus. The separate question is whether the finished model still holds them. If it does, every copy of the weights that is distributed or imported can infringe, wherever the training ran.

### UK: Getty Images v. Stability AI
High Court, 4 Nov 2025, [2025] EWHC 2863 (Ch). Getty dropped its training claim because it had no evidence that training took place in the UK, which left secondary infringement: importing an "infringing copy". The judge accepted that an article can be intangible, but held that Stable Diffusion's weights never stored or reproduced Getty's images, so the model is not an infringing copy. Getty won only narrow trade mark points over watermarks from older versions. On 16 Dec 2025 Getty was granted permission to appeal the secondary infringement ruling; Stability was refused permission on the trade mark findings.

### Germany: GEMA v. OpenAI
Munich Regional Court I, 11 Nov 2025. Lyrics of nine German songs memorised by GPT-4 and GPT-4o were reproduced in the model and in its outputs. The TDM exception covers copies made to build the corpus, not memorisation, and OpenAI rather than its users answered for outputs from simple prompts. OpenAI has appealed.

### Governance takeaway
Test for memorisation and regurgitation before release, and record where training ran.
term:Model Weights as Copies (Getty vs..exam_tip: Getty (UK): weights that never stored the works are not an infringing copy. GEMA (Munich): memorised lyrics are reproductions in the model that the TDM exception does not cover. Both are on appeal, so match each holding to its court rather than treating either as settled.

term:Patent (AI Inventorship).deep_dive:
A patent protects an invention that is novel, useful and non-obvious (35 U.S.C. §§101 to 103). In exchange for publishing how the invention works, the owner gets a limited monopoly, generally 20 years from filing. That bargain is the opposite of a trade secret: you disclose, and in return you can stop others from practising the invention.

AI raises three patent questions.

**Inventorship.** *Thaler v. Vidal* (Fed. Cir., 5 August 2022) held that the Patent Act requires an inventor to be a natural person. The court read 35 U.S.C. §100(f), which defines an inventor as the individual who invented or discovered the subject matter, and rejected DABUS, an AI system named as sole inventor. The USPTO and the EPO agree; South Africa is the outlier that granted a DABUS patent. The lesson for AI-assisted invention is that a human must contribute to the conception, and the USPTO's guidance asks for a significant human contribution.

**Training on patented material.** Using patented algorithms or patented data in training is a separate licensing question from copyright, and it needs its own diligence.

**Disclosure tension.** Patenting an AI-related invention forces you to describe it, which can conflict with keeping the model architecture secret. That is a real strategic choice, not a formality.

Contrast with copyright: copyright protects expression and arises automatically; a patent protects ideas and function and requires examination. The same invention can be handled either way, and the choice trades secrecy against enforceability.
term:Patent (AI Inventorship).exam_tip: An AI system cannot be named inventor: Thaler v. Vidal (Fed. Cir. 2022) rejected DABUS. Do not mix up inventorship (patent, Thaler v. Vidal) with authorship (copyright, Thaler v. Perlmutter): same plaintiff, same conclusion, different statute and court.

term:South Korea AI Basic Act.deep_dive:
### What it is

Officially the Framework Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and Establishment of Trust; BOK v2.1 calls it the South Korean AI Basic Law. The National Assembly passed it on 26 Dec 2024, it was promulgated as **Act No. 20676** on **21 Jan 2025**, and it took effect with its Enforcement Decree (Presidential Decree No. 36053) on **22 Jan 2026**, one year later. Act No. 21311 (20 Jan 2026) amended it.

### Scope

- **Regulator:** the **Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT)** confirms high-impact status, runs fact-finding, issues corrective orders and imposes fines. The Presidential Council on National AI Strategy deliberates on policy and has no enforcement power.
- **Reach:** conduct abroad that affects the Korean market or users in Korea (Art. 4(1)).
- **Exclusion:** AI developed and used solely for national defense or national security (Art. 4(2)).
- **Who is regulated:** AI business operators, government bodies included.

### Shape

Most articles build promotion machinery (a Basic Plan every three years, the AI Safety Institute, data, SME and cluster support). Chapter 4 adds trust duties for generative, high-impact and very high-compute AI. It has no banned-practices list and no conformity assessment, the two EU AI Act contrasts items test most.
term:South Korea AI Basic Act.exam_tip: An option claiming Korea bans social scoring or requires conformity assessment is wrong; the Act has neither. MSIT is the regulator (the privacy regulator PIPC and the presidential council are distractors), and duties started 22 Jan 2026, one year after promulgation.

term:Korea AI Basic Act Fines (Art. 43).deep_dive:
### The three finable failures

Under Art. 43, MSIT can impose an administrative fine of up to **KRW 30 million** (roughly US$21,000 to 22,000), and only for:

1. failing to give users **advance notice** that a product or service uses high-impact or generative AI (Art. 31(1));
2. failing to designate a required **domestic representative** (Art. 36(1));
3. ignoring an MSIT **suspension or corrective order** (Art. 40(3)).

### Everything else goes through an order first

Output labeling, the realistic-content notice, the high-compute safety duties and the Art. 34 high-impact measures are not directly finable. MSIT runs fact-finding under Art. 40, demanding data and inspecting offices, then orders the operator to stop or correct. A fine follows only if the operator ignores that order. The Art. 33 high-impact review and the best-efforts impact assessment fall under neither article. Individuals get no private right of action, though a complaint can prompt fact-finding.

### Grace period

MSIT announced that for at least one year from 22 Jan 2026 it will generally defer fact-finding and fines, except in serious cases such as loss of life or human-rights violations. The duties themselves have applied since day one.

### EU contrast

EU AI Act fines reach EUR 35M or 7% of worldwide turnover.
term:Korea AI Basic Act Fines (Art. 43).exam_tip: The cap is a flat KRW 30 million, with no turnover percentage. term:Algorithmic Disgorgement.deep_dive:
### What the remedy does

In an order under FTC Act section 5, the FTC can require a company to delete the data it obtained unlawfully **and** any model, algorithm or product built from that data. Deleting only the raw data would let the company keep the trained model, and with it the value of the violation. Study material also calls it model deletion.

### AI precedents

- **Everalbum (final May 2021):** a photo app switched face recognition on by default despite telling users otherwise and kept photos of users who had deactivated their accounts. The order required deletion of the photos and of the face-recognition models and algorithms built from them, plus express consent before using face recognition.
- **Rite Aid (Dec 2023):** after years of untested in-store facial recognition, Rite Aid had to delete the images and the algorithms and products developed from them, and tell third parties to delete them too.

### Governance angle

Disgorgement puts the model at risk whenever its training data was collected without notice, consent or a lawful basis. Lineage records tying each model version to its training datasets and the permission behind each let a team show the data was lawful and, if an order comes, scope what must be deleted and retrained.
term:Algorithmic Disgorgement.exam_tip: When a stem has a regulator ordering deletion of the models and algorithms, as well as the data, the answer is algorithmic disgorgement. Tie it to FTC section 5 orders such as Everalbum and Rite Aid, and keep it apart from the GDPR Art. 17 right to erasure.

term:Operation AI Comply.deep_dive:
### The sweep

On **25 Sep 2024** the FTC announced five actions against companies that made deceptive AI claims or used AI to deceive:

- **DoNotPay** sold a robot lawyer it had not tested against the work of a human lawyer; it agreed to pay **$193,000** and stop unsupported claims.
- **Rytr** offered an AI writing tool with a testimonial and review feature that could generate detailed fake reviews.
- **Ascend Ecom, Ecommerce Empire Builders and FBA Machine** sold business opportunities promising that AI-powered online storefronts would earn large incomes; court orders halted the schemes.

Then-Chair Lina Khan said the cases showed there is no AI exemption from existing law.

### What changed in 2025

On **22 Dec 2025** the FTC reopened and set aside the Rytr order. It found the complaint did not support a section 5 violation and that the order unduly burdened AI innovation, citing America's AI Action Plan. The FTC now targets fraud and tangible consumer harm rather than tools that someone might misuse. Deceptive claims about what AI can do are still enforced: in April 2025 the FTC ordered **Workado** to back up its claim that its AI content detector was 98% accurate.

### Governance takeaway

Hold test evidence for every AI capability or accuracy claim before marketing publishes it.
term:Operation AI Comply.exam_tip: Unsupported AI accuracy or capability claims are the live section 5 theory (DoNotPay, Workado). The Rytr set-aside dropped the case against a tool that others might misuse; AI deception remains unlawful.

term:America's AI Action Plan (2025).deep_dive:
### Origin

On **23 Jan 2025** the President signed **EO 14179**, Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence, which called for an AI action plan. The White House published *Winning the Race: America's AI Action Plan* in **July 2025**. It lists recommended policy actions for federal agencies and places no duties on private companies.

### Three pillars

1. Accelerate AI innovation.
2. Build American AI infrastructure.
3. Lead in international AI diplomacy and security.

### Actions that reach the AIGP syllabus

- **NIST AI RMF:** Commerce, through NIST, is to revise the framework to remove references to misinformation, diversity, equity and inclusion, and climate change. NIST says the revision is under way and the Playbook will be updated after it. The exam (BOK v2.1) still tests AI RMF 1.0 as published.
- **FTC:** review investigations opened under the previous administration, and modify or set aside final orders and consent decrees that unduly burden AI innovation. The December 2025 set-aside of the Rytr order cited this.
- **States:** OMB is to have agencies with AI-related discretionary funding weigh a state's AI regulatory climate, a thread EO 14365 took further in December 2025.

### Related order

EO 14148 (20 Jan 2025) revoked EO 14110, the 2023 order that produced NIST AI 600-1.

term:Illinois AI Video Interview Act.deep_dive:
### The duties

The **Artificial Intelligence Video Interview Act** (820 ILCS 42, Public Act 101-0260) took effect **1 Jan 2020**. An employer that asks applicants for **Illinois-based positions** to record video interviews and uses AI to analyze them must, before asking for the video:

1. **notify** the applicant that AI may be used to analyze the interview;
2. **explain** how the AI works and what general characteristics it uses to evaluate applicants;
3. obtain the applicant's **consent**.

Without consent, AI may not evaluate the applicant. The employer may share the videos only with people whose expertise is needed to evaluate the applicant, and on request must **delete them within 30 days**, including copies and backups held by anyone it shared them with.

### Demographic reporting

Since **1 Jan 2022** (Public Act 102-0047), an employer that relies **solely** on AI to decide who advances to an in-person interview must report applicants' race and ethnicity to the Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity (DCEO) each year by 31 Dec. DCEO then reports on any racial bias by 1 Jul.

### Gaps and its partner law

The Act has no penalty or enforcement section. Illinois HB 3773 (in force 2026) covers all employer AI with an effect-based discrimination ban, a zip-code proxy ban and notice.
term:Illinois AI Video Interview Act.exam_tip: An employer running AI on recorded interviews for Illinois jobs must notify, explain and obtain consent before the interview, and delete within 30 days of a request. Keep it apart from HB 3773, the 2026 effect standard for all employer AI.

term:Biometric Information Privacy Act (.deep_dive:
### Scope

The **Biometric Information Privacy Act** (740 ILCS 14, 2008) covers biometric identifiers (retina or iris scans, fingerprints, voiceprints, scans of hand or face geometry) and information derived from them. Facial-recognition and voice-cloning systems that capture them are in scope.

### Duties on private entities

- a public written policy with a retention schedule: destroy the data when the purpose is met or within **3 years** of the person's last interaction, whichever comes first;
- before collection, written notice of the purpose and retention period, and a **written release** from the person;
- no selling, leasing or otherwise **profiting** from biometric data;
- disclosure only with consent or legal compulsion;
- reasonable, industry-standard security.

### Private right of action

Any aggrieved person can sue for liquidated damages of **$1,000 per negligent** or **$5,000 per intentional or reckless** violation (or actual damages if higher), plus fees and injunctions. That combination is what fuels BIPA class actions.

### 2024 amendment

Public Act 103-0769 (effective **2 Aug 2024**): repeated collection of the same identifier from the same person by the same method is one violation with at most one recovery, and an electronic signature counts as a written release.

### AI angle

Collecting Illinois residents' face or voice data to build or run a recognition model needs written releases first.

term:California SB 243 (Companion Chatbo.deep_dive:
### Scope

**SB 243** (Chapter 677, signed 13 Oct 2025) took effect **1 Jan 2026**. A companion chatbot gives adaptive, human-like responses and can meet a user's social needs across interactions. Customer-service bots, limited video-game characters and voice assistants that do not sustain a relationship are excluded.

### Operator duties

- a clear notice that the chatbot is AI wherever a reasonable person could be misled into thinking they are talking to a human;
- a protocol that prevents suicidal-ideation and self-harm content and refers at-risk users to crisis services, published on the operator's website;
- for users the operator knows are minors: disclosure that they are talking to AI, a default reminder at least every **3 hours** to take a break, and reasonable measures to block sexually explicit visuals;
- an annual report to the Office of Suicide Prevention from **1 Jul 2027**, with no personal data.

### Enforcement

Anyone injured can sue for an injunction, the greater of actual damages or **$1,000 per violation**, and attorney fees. Most US AI laws leave enforcement to the attorney general.

### Related laws

Colorado HB 26-1263 (duties from 1 Jan 2027) also requires a crisis-referral self-harm protocol, with annual reports to the AG. California added SB 1119 (signed 10 Sep 2026) with further child-safety rules for companion chatbots.
term:California SB 243 (Companion Chatbo.exam_tip: SB 243 is one of only two laws in this area with a private right of action (BIPA is the other). When a stem pairs it with Colorado HB 26-1263, the shared duty is a self-harm protocol that refers users to crisis services.

term:Illinois SB 315 (AI Safety Measures.deep_dive:
### Thresholds

The **Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act** (SB 315, Public Act 104-0538) was signed 6 Jul 2026 and takes effect **1 Jan 2027**. It uses California SB 53's numbers: a frontier model is trained with more than **10^26** operations, and a large frontier developer had more than **$500 million** in revenue.

### Duties by date

- **From 1 Jan 2027:** a large frontier developer needs a current **disclosure statement** on file with the Illinois Emergency Management Agency and Office of Homeland Security (IEMA-OHS), renewed annually, to develop, deploy or operate frontier models in Illinois. Failures cost $1,000 per day.
- **From 1 Jan 2028:** large frontier developers publish and follow a **frontier AI framework** and **hire an independent third party every year to audit compliance**, publishing a summary within 30 days.
- **Incidents:** report to IEMA-OHS and the AG within **72 hours** of learning facts that support a reasonable belief one occurred, or within 24 hours to an appropriate authority if there is imminent danger.

### Enforcement

The AG enforces exclusively: up to **$1M** for a first violation and **$3M** for later ones. No private right of action; employees get whistleblower protections.

### The trio compared

California: 15-day incident reports, no audit. New York: 72 hours, no audit. Illinois: 72 hours plus the audit.

term:Copyright Office AI Reports (Parts.deep_dive:
The US Copyright Office published its Copyright and Artificial Intelligence report in three parts. The reports set out the Office's analysis and recommendations; courts are not bound by them.

- **Part 1, Digital Replicas (31 July 2024):** recommends a new federal law against unauthorised digital replicas that realistically but falsely depict a person.
- **Part 2, Copyrightability (29 January 2025):** existing law is flexible enough. Output is protected only where a human determined sufficient expressive elements, through human work perceptible in the output or creative selection, arrangement or modification. Prompts alone do not give enough control over the expression. Using AI as a tool does not bar protection of the human contribution, and no new right for AI output is needed.
- **Part 3, Generative AI Training (9 May 2025, pre-publication; the final version is expected without substantive change):** several stages of training implicate the exclusive rights, so fair use is the key question, decided case by case. Many training uses are likely transformative, but commercial use of vast troves of works to produce expressive content that competes with them, especially through illegal access, goes beyond established fair use boundaries. Factor four should not be read narrowly, so market dilution by AI output of the same kind counts. The Office favours voluntary licensing and calls government intervention premature.
term:Copyright Office AI Reports (Parts.exam_tip: Match the part to the question: digital replicas (Part 1), authorship of outputs (Part 2), training and fair use (Part 3). Part 3's red flag is commercial use of illegally accessed works to make competing content, and it rejects a narrow reading of market harm.

term:Four-Fifths Rule.deep_dive:
### The calculation
Divide each group's selection rate by the rate of the group selected most often. Under the 1978 Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures (29 CFR 1607.4(D)), the federal enforcement agencies generally treat a ratio below 0.8 as evidence of adverse impact. Example: women selected at 36% and men at 50% gives 0.72, below the line.

### Limits written into the rule
- Smaller differences can still be adverse impact where they are significant in both statistical and practical terms.
- Larger differences may not count where they rest on small numbers and are not statistically significant.

So the ratio starts an inquiry. It does not decide a Title VII case, which still runs through the §703(k) steps: job relatedness and business necessity, then any less discriminatory alternative the employer refuses.

### Where it shows up in AI governance
Bias testing of hiring models reports impact ratios, and 0.8 is the usual screening reference in US employment analytics. NYC Local Law 144 requires the same impact-ratio arithmetic in its bias audits but sets no pass or fail threshold, so calling a ratio under 0.8 a Local Law 144 violation is wrong. The disparity can still create exposure under federal or state anti-discrimination law.
term:Four-Fifths Rule.exam_tip: Expect arithmetic: divide by the highest group's rate and compare with 0.8. Below 0.8 means potential adverse impact to investigate, not proof of discrimination, and it is not a Local Law 144 pass or fail line.

term:Proxy Discrimination.deep_dive:
### How it happens
A model never shown race, sex or age can still learn them from features that correlate with them. The vault's examples: postal code for race, socioeconomic status or religion; education level for income or nationality; occupation for gender or class; credit history for race through systemic inequality. Amazon abandoned a resume-screening model in 2018 after it learned, from mostly male historical resumes, to penalise graduates of women's colleges.

### How the law treats it
- **Disparate treatment:** choosing a feature because it stands in for a protected class is intentional discrimination. ECOA still bars deliberate use of prohibited-basis proxies after Regulation B dropped the effects test (effective 21 July 2026).
- **Disparate impact:** an unintended proxy that produces a disproportionate effect is judged under an impact standard such as Title VII §703(k) or the Fair Housing Act.
- **State law:** Illinois HB 3773, in force from 1 January 2026, bars employers from using zip codes as a proxy for protected classes in AI-assisted employment decisions.

### Controls
Test features for correlation with protected classes, run disparate-impact metrics on outputs, document the business justification for any strongly correlated feature, and look for a less discriminatory alternative before keeping it. Removing the sensitive column alone is no defence.
term:Proxy Discrimination.exam_tip: When a stem says the model never uses race but leans on postal code, the answer is proxy discrimination with disparate-impact exposure. The correct response is to test, document a business justification and seek a less discriminatory alternative; deleting the protected attribute alone fails.

term:Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA).deep_dive:
### Why AI teams run into it
A consumer report is any communication by a consumer reporting agency bearing on a person's creditworthiness, character, general reputation, personal characteristics or mode of living, used or expected to be used in deciding eligibility for credit, insurance, employment or another permissible purpose (15 U.S.C. 1681a(d)). A vendor selling an algorithmic score built from third-party data for those decisions can be a consumer reporting agency, and its score a consumer report.

### Duties to know
- **Accuracy and disputes:** consumer data must be accurate, and consumers can dispute errors.
- **Employment use (1681b(b)):** a clear, standalone written disclosure and the candidate's written authorisation before the report is obtained, then a copy of the report and a summary of rights before any adverse action.
- **Adverse action (1681m):** notice of the action, the credit score used, the agency's contact details, a statement that the agency did not make the decision, and the right to a free report and to dispute it.

### Status
CFPB Circular 2024-06 (background dossiers and algorithmic scores in employment) was withdrawn on 12 May 2025; the statute did not change.

### Versus ECOA
FCRA addresses where decision data comes from and whether it is accurate. ECOA addresses discrimination in credit and the specific reasons for a denial.
term:Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA).exam_tip: Choose FCRA when the stem is about third-party consumer data feeding a decision, including employment screening with credit reports; choose ECOA when it is about discrimination or the reasons for a credit denial. A withdrawn CFPB circular does not remove FCRA duties.

term:AI Stakeholder Roles (ISO/IEC 22989.deep_dive:
ISO/IEC 22989 Clause 5.19 sorts everyone around an AI system into six roles, each with named sub-roles.

| Role | Sub-roles |
|---|---|
| AI provider | AI platform provider; AI product or service provider |
| AI producer | AI developer |
| AI customer | AI user |
| AI partner | AI system integrator; data provider; AI auditor; AI evaluator |
| AI subject | data subject; other subjects |
| Relevant authorities | policy makers; regulators |

### Why the roles matter
- **ISO/IEC 42001 Clause 4.1** requires an organization to determine its roles for the AI systems it develops, provides or uses, and points to 22989 for the role descriptions. The roles it holds shape which Annex A controls it applies.
- One organization can hold several roles at once. A firm that builds a model and sells access to it is both producer and provider.

### Not the EU AI Act's roles
The ISO roles are descriptive and carry no legal duties. The AI Act's provider (Art. 3(3)) covers what ISO splits into producer and provider, the deployer (Art. 3(4)) is closest to the customer, and affected persons line up with subjects. Partners have no AI Act category of their own: an integrator's duties depend on the facts, and Art. 25 can make it a provider.

term:AI System Life Cycle (ISO/IEC 22989.deep_dive:
ISO/IEC 22989 Clause 6 gives a reference life cycle for AI systems. Its stages, in order:

- **Inception**: set objectives and requirements, and judge feasibility, including whether AI fits the problem.
- **Design and development**: acquire and prepare data, design the model, train and tune it.
- **Verification and validation**: confirm the system meets its specification and suits its intended use.
- **Deployment**: install and release it into the target environment.
- **Operation and monitoring**: run it and track its performance.
- **Continuous validation**: only for systems that keep learning in production; checks that the learning has not broken the requirements.
- **Re-evaluation**: review whether the system still meets its objectives.
- **Retirement**: decommission or replace the system and archive or dispose of its models and data.

### Where it is reused
- ISO/IEC 23894 Annex C maps risk management activities onto these stages.
- ISO/IEC 42001 Annex A.6 controls cover the AI system life cycle.

### Exam traps
Study notes often use other labels: adoption for inception, design and construction for design and development, reassessment for re-evaluation, decommissioning for retirement. The NIST AI RMF lifecycle uses its own stage names, from plan and design through operate and monitor, so match the vocabulary to the framework the question names.
term:AI System Life Cycle (ISO/IEC 22989.exam_tip: Know the order and the conditional stage: verification and validation comes before deployment, and continuous validation applies only to systems that keep learning in production. Other labels map across: adoption is inception, reassessment is re-evaluation, decommissioning is retirement.

term:Personal Data.deep_dive:
ISO/IEC 22989 defines personal data broadly: **all information that can be used to identify the natural person** to whom it relates, or that is or could be directly or indirectly related to a natural person. The trailing clause is the important one. It reaches information that is not itself an identifier but points at a person, which is how most AI training data becomes personal data.

### The statutory anchor

Article 4(1) of the GDPR defines personal data as any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person, and treats identifiability as reaching anyone who can be singled out, directly or indirectly, by reference to an identifier or to factors specific to them. The two definitions line up, and the ISO note says so: it is aligned with privacy regulation concepts.

Three consequences follow for AI:

- **Training corpora are usually personal data.** Web text, logs, support tickets and images generally contain information relating to identifiable people, so the GDPR's processing rules attach before any model is trained.
- **Derived data stays personal.** Inferences about a person are information relating to them. A model that predicts health status from purchase history is processing special-category data under Article 9 even though nobody collected a health record.
- **Synthetic and aggregated data need care.** Aggregation does not automatically anonymise, and anonymisation is a high bar because re-identification by combination is always possible in principle.

### The exam distinction

Personal data is defined by relation to a person, not by the label on a field. If a fact can be linked to an identifiable individual, directly or indirectly, it is personal data and the lawful-basis, purpose-limitation and rights machinery applies.
term:Personal Data.exam_tip: Personal data (EU, Art. 4(1)) is wider than PII (US): indirect identifiability and inferred attributes count, so Art. 9 can reach data never collected. A trained model is not automatically anonymous; apply the EDPB Opinion 28/2024 extraction-and-query test.

term:ISO/IEC 23894.deep_dive:
ISO/IEC 23894:2023 carries three informative annexes, and Annex B is the one that catalogues **AI risk sources**: the origins of risk an organization should look for when it identifies AI-related risks. Annex A lists common AI-related objectives, and Annex C maps the risk-management process onto the AI system life cycle (inception, design and development, verification and validation, deployment, operation and monitoring, retirement).

The risk sources cluster around where AI risk actually comes from: the data (quality, provenance, representativeness), the model (behaviour, performance, uncertainty, drift), the deployment context and use case, the interaction with people and society, and the legal and regulatory environment. That is why 23894's risk-identification clause tells organizations to consider design and development, data quality and provenance, model behaviour, deployment context, stakeholder impacts and the regulatory environment together.

Two framing points matter for the exam. The annexes are **informative**, not normative: they guide, they do not create auditable requirements. And 23894's definition of risk follows ISO 31000, the effect of uncertainty on objectives, so a risk source can produce upside as well as downside. Annex B is the AI-specific content that distinguishes 23894 from the generic standard it extends.
term:ISO/IEC 23894.exam_tip: Extends ISO 31000 and is guidance, so there is nothing to certify. It asks what threatens the organization's objectives, upside included; 42005 asks how a system affects people. It is not one of BOK v2.1's three core ISO standards (22989, 42001, 42005).
